#2797. $180 million Van Gogh tests the art market and collector confidence

A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions straight to your inbox.

The art auctions in New York next week could top $2 billion, as a treasure trove of masterpieces comes to the market for the first time in decades.

Total sales at Sotheby's, Christie's and Phillips are expected to be around $2.4 billion, which would equal last year's total, according to ArtTactic. Sotheby's alone is expected to pull in over $1.1 billion, with a single collection from The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection estimated at $450 million.

The collection includes the two big headliners of the week: Vincent van Gogh's landscape "Châtaigniers en fleurs," (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million and Paul Cézanne's "Arlequin," estimated at $120 million. Neither has been seen in public for a half a century.

Sotheby's CEO Charles Stewart said demand is strong in the art market, especially for the highest quality blue-chip works, as rising stocks markets and private wealth boost the confidence of collectors.

"There's been enormous wealth creation and a lot of confidence in markets," Stewart said. "It's a global phenomenon. We're seeing recovery and greater interest across Asia and something really exciting happening from the Middle East across to Singapore and Europe and the U.S."

Christie's star of the week is Wassily Kandinsky's "Betonte Ecken," estimated at $60 million to $80 million. Christie's CEO Bonnie Brennan describes the market is "confident but discerning, rewarding truly exceptional works." She said recent gyrations in the stock market and fears of an AI bubble aren't likely to deter serious collectors.

"At the very highest end of our market, collectors tend to take a much longer-term view," Brennan said. "They understand that the opportunity to acquire a masterpiece may come only once in a generation, and that can be far more important than what the stock market has done in any particular week. In uncertain moments, the very best can actually become even more compelling."

The art market has continued to rebound this year after declines in 2023 and 2024, with auction sales in the first half up 70% over last year, to $6.8 billion, according to Bank of America.

Drew Watson, head of art services at Bank of America, said blue-chip art is outperforming, with Impressionist & Modern sales up 133% in the first half.

"Our outlook for the art market this November is cautiously optimistic," Watson said. "Improving liquidity, combined with an unusually strong concentration of fresh-to-market private collections, creates a favorable backdrop for the marquee sales."

Nine regionals feed the national meet, and the top two teams in each race at every regional earn an automatic bid. That adds up to 18 automatic team berths per gender.

Runners can also qualify on their own. At each regional, the first four top-25 finishers who are not on a team already headed to nationals advance automatically. Two more individuals are added at-large, for 38 in all.

The NCAA Cross Country Championships are on Saturday, Nov. 21, at the LaVern Gibson Championship Cross Country Course in Terre Haute, Indiana. The meet airs on ESPNU.

#2793. Heating oil prices are up 59% from last winter. The spike is 'crushing folks,' Maine nonprofit says

Winter heating bills can strain household budgets. This year, a spike in heating oil prices could make the season especially difficult for households that depend on the fuel and have little financial wiggle room.

The national average price of heating oil was roughly $5.91 a gallon as of Nov. 9, up about $2.19, or 59%, from a year earlier, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

In Maine, the average price per gallon is roughly $5.83, up about $2.49 from a year earlier, or about 75%. The state is among those whose residents may feel the price rise acutely — about 50% of homes there use heating oil.

The jump "is crushing folks," said Jason Parent, CEO of AVEC Community Action, a nonprofit agency based in Presque Isle, Maine, that provides heating assistance and other social services in three of the state's 16 counties. Many residents face immediate crises, he said, such as empty fuel tanks or reliance on unsafe heating sources.

"My fear is that there are households out there who have secondary fuel sources like wood stoves, pellet stoves and other things that are no longer operating and functioning in a safe way," Parent said.

The price surge comes on the heels of years of high overall inflation that has already squeezed household budgets, he said.

"The cost of living has made it impossible for households who had been figuring out how to get by without [financial help]," Parent said.

The price spike comes amid a tight global market for refined fuels, a category that includes heating oil and diesel. Supply shocks tied to the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war, low inventories and limited refining capacity have constrained supplies and added upward pressure on fuel prices, according to recent research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City.

The EIA predicts that a warmer winter in the Northeast will reduce consumption, helping to offset higher prices. In October, the agency forecast that the average household using heating oil will spend $2,115 from November through March, about 21% more than last year.

Meanwhile, homes primarily heated with natural gas are expected to spend an average of $640 this winter, down 9%, while those using propane are forecast to spend an average of $1,246, down 3%, according to the EIA's October forecast. Households using electricity for heating are expected to spend an average of $1,196, up 4% from a year ago. These are national figures.

Roughly 4.1 million U.S. households use heating oil as their primary means of heating their homes, according to the EIA. Most of them — close to 3.4 million — are located in the Northeast.

Unlike electricity or natural gas, heating oil is delivered in large quantities. Payment terms vary, but some dealers require a minimum delivery or charge extra for smaller orders. In Maine, for example, ordering at least 100 gallons for a standard 275-gallon tank can avoid a surcharge, according to the state attorney general's office. At current prices, that 100 gallons would cost about $600 — a tall order for some households.

AVEC's Home Energy Assistance Program, or HEAP, provides financial assistance to qualifying households, based primarily on income and the number of people living in the home. Funding originates with the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP, which is run by the U.S. Health and Human Services Department and overseen by state agencies, often working with local organizations such as AVEC.

Maine and tribal grantees in the state received about $38 million from LIHEAP in October, according to a press release from outgoing Republican Sen. Susan Collins. AVEC administers about $4 million of that through HEAP, Parent said. AVEC also gets donations from community fundraising to help residents cover heating costs.

A component of HEAP is the Energy Crisis Intervention Program, which serves qualifying families who face an energy crisis, such as a potential electric shutoff or an empty oil tank and no financial means to replenish the supply.

AVEC began taking calls for that program on Nov. 2, Parent said.

"In the first hour alone, there were 150 voicemail messages on our emergency fuel line," Parent said. "People were in crisis before the program opened up."

Catherine Lafleche of Hersey, Maine, describes AVEC as a lifeline.

The 65-year-old is guardian to two grandchildren, ages 11 and 6, and is living mostly on about $1,100 in monthly Social Security benefits and state guardianship assistance, after shattering her upper-arm bone in a fall in April. Her injury required reverse shoulder replacement surgery, from which she continues to recover. Before that fall, she had worked as a substitute teacher and bookkeeper.

"I'm $6,000 short of income at this point in the year," Lafleche said.

Hersey is in Maine's northernmost county, Aroostook, where January and February bring average high temperatures in the 20s and average lows in the single digits, based on National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data from 1991 to 2020 recorded at a Caribou Municipal Airport weather station. Last winter, the area experienced severe cold snaps, including on Jan. 24, when the high was minus 2 degrees Fahrenheit.

Lafleche applied to HEAP through AVEC in August, but a backlog meant potentially waiting until November for assistance. Unable to afford more fuel when it became chilly, she ran out of heating oil in early October and relied on a small wood stove to keep part of her house warm, burning Amazon boxes collected from other local residents because she didn't have enough firewood.

In late October, an AVEC representative called to say a charitable donation would cover 100 gallons of heating oil.

"When the oil man came, I cried," Lafleche said.

For residents in Maine who need help covering the cost to heat their homes and are seeking out help, "the need is outpacing the benefits," said Parent, of AVEC.

The average benefit through HEAP is about $750 per household this season, up from roughly $550 a year ago, Parent said. "That $750 is going less far than the $550 did last season" for heating oil, he said. "It's buying fewer gallons because of the precipitous increase."

The benefits are generally paid directly to the fuel supplier as a credit on the household's account. Even if a household qualifies, funding may run out.

"We're in a world of hurt now ... but it's going to be crisis time again in January or February," Parent said.

The Trump administration, in an effort to bring down heating oil prices, said it would release 300,000 barrels of heating oil from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve, according to a Nov. 4 release from the U.S. Energy Department.

Whether adding this extra heating oil to the market will reduce prices for residents depends at least partly on how it gets doled out, said Jonathan Rubin, director of the Margaret Chase Smith Policy Center and a professor of economics at the University of Maine.

"No one really knows the economic impact, because will the home-heating oil distributors release it in one month, which would make it about 10% to 12% of a single month's supply? Or will they release it over the entire season, in which case it's only about one and a half percent of the entire season's home heating oil supply?" Rubin said.

"I would say that this is a modest short-term buffer," he said.

Congressional lawmakers have called for increased LIHEAP funding this year due to rising energy costs, including heating oil. Dozens of House lawmakers — mostly Democrats — signed an Oct. 14 letter to the House Appropriations Committee seeking an additional $3 billion in emergency supplemental funding for LIHEAP.

That followed an Oct. 1 letter from a group of Democratic senators and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., to Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of the Health and Human Services, also asking that he seek at least $3 billion more for LIHEAP.

Already, the government released roughly $3.63 billion in LIHEAP funding nationwide on Oct. 9 — 90% of the roughly $4 billion available under a continuing resolution that is currently funding federal agencies.

The timing for disbursing the remainder depends on when Congress either passes full-year funding for the 2027 fiscal year — which started Oct. 1 and runs through Sept. 30, 2027 — or passes another stopgap measure to keep the government running. If lawmakers do neither by Dec. 11, a federal shutdown would begin.

Whether the additional $3 billion requested for LIHEAP will be considered in any upcoming congressional appropriations process is uncertain.

Lafleche, the Hersey resident, said the 100 gallons of heating oil donated to her, along with some firewood she has now purchased, should keep her home warm until early December. She hopes to receive approval for benefits by then through HEAP, which has helped her in past years.

"We're not in this position by choice. Most of us made every plan to the contrary, but it stacked up to be not enough. And I feel like we don't deserve to be cold," she said.

#2792. Draymond Green defends Rockets from ‘dirty' label after Steph Curry injury

Draymond Green defends Rockets from 'dirty' label after Steph Curry injury originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

Draymond Green does not think the Houston Rockets are a dirty team. He does, however, believe they are a very physical one.

Speaking on "The Draymond Green Show" as he discussed Steph Curry's injury and playing without him, Green addressed the label that followed the Warriors' 115-108 loss in Houston on Nov. 11. Curry grimaced and reached for his right side after tangling with Rockets center Alperen Sengun on a screen early in the first quarter, leaving the game minutes later.

"I know a lot of people are saying, 'Oh man, the Houston Rockets are a dirty team.' I don't get off into that dirty thing," Green said. "Every now and then you see some people that just do things that are downright dirty, and it happens, and when it does, I'll speak on it."

Wednesday's game saw Rockets guard Marcus Smart ejected for throwing a punch that grazed the nose of Warriors center Charles Bassey, and the NBA suspended Smart three games. Bassey said Smart was playing dirty "the whole game" and called the punch "fake toughness."

Green drew a different line. He said the thing that bothers him most about Houston is not rough play.

"Do they do some bulls— when we play them? Absolutely," Green said. "I think the thing that may irritate me the most is, like, they play super physical, but then they start flopping sometimes, you know. "When we were watching film pregame, you can see on the film they are physical as hell, and so give them credit," Green said.

#2790. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2786. Trump doesn’t plan to raise Nvidia, spy issue during China trip: U.S. officials

President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.

Officials also said that Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."

"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.

Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."

China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.

Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed, a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.

The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.

During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.

"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.

"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

#2785. Episcopal School of Dallas leans on defense, defeats Arlington Oakridge for state title

DALLAS – Episcopal School of Dallas finished off an undefeated season in thrilling fashion, getting a fourth quarter 1-yard go-ahead touchdown catch by John Edge Sowa and a game-sealing interception by Daniel Hoffpauir with 1:03 remaining to claim a 14-10 victory over Arlington Oakridge in the SPC 3A State Championship game on Saturday night at Gene & Jerry Jones Family Stadium.

Episcopal School of Dallas (11-0) leaned heavily on a big-play defense to secure the state title win, forcing four turnovers and having 10 stops for loss in the win.

"We knew it wasn't going to be easy and that the game would come down to the fourth quarter," Episcopal School of Dallas head coach Bob Benson said. "The defense made a lot of big plays tonight and gave us a chance to win in the final minutes."

That chance to win came with 4:45 remaining to play, as a strip sack and fumble recovery by Sowa set up ESD at the Oakridge 30. A key 27-yard catch-and-run by Nico Marquez put the ball at the Oakridge 1, with Sowa snagging a high throw from Miles Link one play later for at 14-10 lead with 3:36 remaining.

Arlington Oakridge (9-2) got the ball back and drove to near midfield on its ensuing possession but was turned away on 4th and six on a sack by ESD's Beckett Concors with 2:14 to play.

ESD would be forced to punt to give Oakridge the ball at its on 4-yard line with 1:38 remaining, with its defense answering the call one last time on the Hoffpauir interception to allow the offense to run out the clock.

Oakridge struck first in the title game on the opening drive, moving inside the ESD 5 before settling for a 22-yard field goal by Will Lemonds.

ESD didn't wait long to respond, as Marquez raced 65 yards on the opening play of the ensuing drive to give ESD a 7-3 lead with 7:46 left in the opening quarter. Marquez had a solid game for ESD, rushing for a game-high 121 yards.

The defenses for both teams then took control for the rest of the first half, with each team forcing a pair of turnovers. Both ESD turnovers were crucial stops, coming on a pair of red-zone interceptions by Wayte McKnight.

While ESD could not take advantage of the turnovers, they maintained its four-point advantage going into the half.

In the third quarter, Oakridge continued to press ESD and had a key shot to retake the lead after getting first and goal at the ESD 10 on its opening drive of the half.

However, the ESD defense turned Oakridge back on a fourth and goal stand, taking over at its own 1-yard line with 3:50 left in the third quarter.

Oakridge's defense then stepped up, forcing a fumble on the next play that was recovered by Tyson Dean to take a 10-7 lead before leading to the final thrilling minutes of the contest.

#2784. Phoenix might be figuring things out, one stop at a time

Need a little hope? Looking for something to give you those warm and fuzzies as you sip your morning coffee? The sugar and cream aren't doing enough to brighten your day? Well, for all the ugly statistics we've been compiling about the Phoenix Suns lately, here's one that might make that coffee taste a little sweeter.

Through the first six games of the regular season, Phoenix ranked dead last in the NBA in defensive rating, surrendering a staggering 124.5 points per 100 possessions. It was an atrocious start, one that had us questioning whether this team possessed the personnel, discipline, or defensive identity necessary to compete night in and night out.

But since then? Things have changed considerably. Over their last five games, the Suns have posted a defensive rating of 109.0, the sixth-best mark in the NBA during that stretch. Their net rating has climbed to +4.2, ranking ninth in the league, a significant improvement from the -10.3 net rating that placed them 25th during their first six games.

That's a pretty substantial turnaround in a relatively short period of time.

And perhaps the most encouraging part is that those numbers include the absolute shellacking Phoenix suffered at the hands of the Spurs. Even with that disaster factored into the equation, the Suns have managed to establish themselves as one of the league's more effective defensive teams over their last five outings.

Now, does that mean all their problems have magically disappeared? Of course not. The rebounding remains atrocious, the lack of size continues to create significant disadvantages, and the questions surrounding roster construction and player fit aren't going anywhere anytime soon. But there is something encouraging about watching this team begin to stabilize defensively.

Much like last season, Phoenix stumbled out of the gate, struggling to establish any semblance of consistency before gradually finding its footing. And while we're still dealing with a relatively small sample size, the defensive improvement suggests that some of the early growing pains are beginning to subside.

The rotations are becoming more connected. The effort is more consistent. And the Suns are beginning to demonstrate they can make life difficult for opposing offenses, despite the physical limitations that continue to plague this roster.

There's still plenty of work to be done, and nobody should be throwing a parade over five games of improved defensive efficiency. But considering where this team stood after six games, seeing Phoenix climb from the league's worst defensive rating to the sixth-best over its next five is certainly worth acknowledging.

The defense is giving us something to feel good about. Perhaps it's a reminder that sometimes these things take time. I'll be the first to admit that I'm guilty of overreacting. I constantly find myself mining statistics, searching for numbers that either validate what I'm witnessing while watching these basketball games or challenge the conclusions I've already started forming. That's always the fascinating part of analyzing sports. There's the eye test, there's the data test, and somewhere in between lies the reality of what's actually happening on the court. And sometimes, multiple things can be true simultaneously.

The Phoenix Suns can be atrocious on the boards while still developing into a good defensive team. Those two realities aren't mutually exclusive, and we're beginning to see evidence of that as Phoenix demonstrates an improved ability to shut down opposing offenses for extended stretches, creating enough separation to secure victories.

The issues with rim deterrence remain, and opposing teams continue to exploit the Suns' lack of size around the basket. But on the perimeter? Things are beginning to look considerably better. Through the first six games of the season, Phoenix was allowing opponents to shoot 40.3% from beyond the arc, the second-worst mark in the NBA. It was a troubling statistic that reflected a defense struggling with rotations, communication, and the ability to consistently contest shots. Since then, that number has dropped to 33.9%, the 10th-best mark in the league during a five-game stretch in which the Suns have gone 4-1.

Part of it can certainly be attributed to regression toward the mean. Opponents were unlikely to continue shooting above 40% from deep indefinitely. But dismissing the entire improvement as statistical normalization would overlook the tangible progress we're witnessing from Phoenix defensively. The individual numbers help illustrate that improvement.

During the first six games, opponents were shooting 46.7% from three against Dillon Brooks. Over the last five, that number has dropped to 37.7%. Still not particularly impressive, but considerably better than what we witnessed during the opening stretch. Miles Bridges, who appeared lost on more than a few defensive rotations early in the season, has experienced a similar improvement. Opponents were shooting 38.1% from beyond the arc against him during the first six games. That number has since fallen to 34.7%.

These aren't insignificant developments. They're signs of players beginning to understand their responsibilities, recognize rotations, and operate with greater cohesion within Jordan Ott's defensive system.

There's another factor contributing to the increased defensive intensity. The bench. Jordan Goodwin has been fantastic over the last two games, bringing the kind of relentless energy and defensive aggression that can completely alter the complexion of a basketball game. Ryan Dunn has also begun making a more noticeable impact, using his length, athleticism, and defensive instincts to disrupt opposing offenses. Together, they've helped give Phoenix something that was desperately missing during the early portion of the season: a second unit capable of changing the momentum of a game through defensive effort.

The numbers reflect that impact. Through the first six games, the Suns' bench posted a net rating of +1.5. Over the last five games, that number has improved to +5.3. That's meaningful progress, particularly for a team whose starting lineup continues to struggle with consistency and finding the right combinations.

The bench has become a catalyst for much of the Suns' recent success, providing the defensive intensity, cohesion, and energy that have helped stabilize a team that looked completely disjointed at the start of the season.

Does five games of improved defensive performance mean Phoenix has solved all its problems? Certainly not. The rebounding remains a disaster, the interior defense still needs significant attention, and the roster continues to present challenges that aren't going to disappear overnight. But perhaps that's the lesson here. As much as we want immediate answers, as much as we want the statistics to confirm our suspicions after every game, sometimes a team needs time to figure out how its pieces fit together. While the Suns are still a work in progress, the defensive numbers suggest that some of those pieces are finally beginning to fall into place.

So go ahead. Take another sip of that coffee.

#2782. Forget what Lane Kiffin says, because LSU is no villain. It's a bust

BATON ROUGE, LA – Arch Manning pointed to the Texas sideline in triumph. He'd made so many mistakes on this night, but he couldn't have been thinking of any of them in this moment.

Not after he'd flicked a game-winning touchdown to Raleek Brown.

As Manning celebrated, Lane Kiffin stood with his hands on his hips and stared toward the opposite end of the field.

It's official. Kiffin's first season is a massive flop, because his team's one reliable trait was its inability to finish games.

LSU is out of the playoff race, with two games to go.

So much hype, so much money spent, such little to show for it.

LSU led for most of the game, but when the clock hit triple zeros, the score said this:

Kiffin's first season on the bayou will end in an irrelevant bowl game.

He'll finish with fewer wins than Brian Kelly secured in his first LSU season.

Texas won despite Manning's three interceptions, despite LSU putting the Texas quarterback in a blender for most of the night.

Because, LSU can't handle the pressures of the fourth quarter..

Not against Mississippi. Not against Kentucky. Not against Alabama. And, not against Texas despite leading all but the final three seconds of the second half.

Kiffin badly wanted to talk a scary LSU super villain into existence, but the Tigers never looked intimidating enough to earn that label.

LSU and Kiffin are Charlie Brown. Lucy took the football away. Again.

Two of the nation's most expensive rosters conducted a contest to see how many turnovers they could rack up between them.

The Tigers head into the final two weeks of the season without a single signature victory on the resume of Kiffin's first season, and we can stop pretending like LSU is a playoff team.

What's the Guv got to say about this one?

Not much. He's on to tweeting about Will Wade's basketball team.

As poorly as Manning played for much of the game, LSU struggled to fully capitalize because Sam Leavitt matched Manning with three interceptions of his own, and LSU wasted a few red-zone opportunities.

A $13 million coach, a $50 million roster, and not one win of substance to show for it.

Kiffin is no big-game coach, and LSU is no fierce villain. It's just a meek antihero that can't stand up to any pressure.

Blake Toppmeyer is the USA TODAY Network's senior national college football columnist. Listen to his podcast, "College Football Unfiltered."Email him at BToppmeyer@gannett.com and follow him on X @btoppmeyer.

#2781. How Nvidia turmoil and a Democratic Congress could reshape the AI trade, according to ETF experts

The largest technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade could stand to benefit the most from Nvidia's woes and a Democratic-controlled Congress pushing back on data centers, according to investing experts interviewed on CNBC's "ETF Edge" earlier this week.

"We may have been put in an environment, as much as investors have sort of been looking for areas outside of Big Tech, where net-net Big Tech ends up as the winner once again," said Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza, whose firm manages the Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS).

Part of his bull case: Other players in the AI trade are positioned to fill Nvidia's chip demand if investors lose trust in the company after a tumultuous week that saw its iconic founder and CEO Jensen Huang resign.

"If we get into an environment where people can't trust … Nvidia, they're going to look for other sources for these chips because they need them," Mazza said during the "ETF Edge" interview, which occurred Monday as the Nvidia scandal grew but before Huang had resigned.

Discussing recent fund flow activity for the MAGS ETF, as well as for the Roundhill Neocloud ETF (NCLD) — which focuses on smaller market cap, specialized cloud computing companies — Mazza said, "In a weird way, [hyperscalers] may continue to benefit from this because they have the compute available. It's going to be more valuable if the demand is there."

The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF ended the week in the green, albeit with a gain of less than 1%, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF was up over 1%, though earnings from top holdings Coreweave and Nebius presented a mixed picture.

CoreWeave had its best day since April 2025 on Wednesday after its latest quarterly results, while Nebius shares sank after its Thursday report. The neocloud ETF remains deeply in the red since its August 2026 launch, down 39%, amid concerns about balance sheet strength, which could linger given Nvidia's role in financing the AI buildout. CoreWeave shares sank again on Friday, and Nvidia posted its longest losing streak since 2012 after its latest weekly losses.

Nvidia's interim CEO and current chief financial officer Colette Kress will have her first opportunity to reassure the market when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," Kress said in a statement issued on Thursday morning when the company announced Huang's exit.

Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives said on "ETF Edge" on Monday that the market will remain optimistic about other AI chip players, like AMD and Alphabet, if Nvidia faces prolonged headwinds. Ives helped create the Dan IVES Wedbush AI Revolution ETF (IVES) while at Wedbush Securities, where he served as the managing director and global head of technology research before departing Wedbush to form his own firm earlier this year.

AMD finished trading this week up close to 13%, with Broadcom posting similar gains.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index posted its best week since August as Nvidia's slump reshuffled the AI trade.

Yorkville Ives lowered its price target on Nvidia to $225 from $300 on Thursday after Huang's resignation, but maintained a buy rating on the stock, which finished the week at $162.85 per share.

"Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," Ives wrote in a note to investors on Thursday. "The strategic roadmap is already essentially built around the next few family of chips and physical AI with 42k employees driving it. ... Valuation at roughly 10x 28 EPS is way too cheap once Nvidia gets through this storm and emerges on the other side."

The compute that does exist could become even more indispensable against the backdrop of a potential slowdown to the data-center buildout by Congress after the Democratic Party gains of Nov. 3 swept control of Congress, Mazza said.

Ives estimates that the "blue tidal wave" in Congress could mean 10% of planned data centers won't materialize on the low end, and 15%-20% on the high end, but he added that demand still outstrips supply four to one. "The compute is just that much more valuable in the capacity today than it was a week ago. So I could argue just more and more bullish, strong, get stronger," Ives said.

"The game is going to change for Big Tech. It will slow it down. But there's no overbuild, no bubble concerns. And I view that as actually a positive thing," he added.

#2779. Virginia Tech football: Stanford shocks Hokies 40-22

The Stanford Cardinal flew across the country to cold, windy Blacksburg, Virginia, and took it to the Virginia Tech Hokies, defeating them 40-22. It was Stanford's first road win since Sept. 2024.

Things started badly for the Hokies early. After gaining around 34 yards on the opening drive, head coach James Franklin went for it on fourth down, and the Hokies couldn't convert. Stanford ball. Fortunately, Tech's defense looked like it came to play early with a couple of stops on the Cardinal's first two drives.

However, everything changed on VT's second drive, when quarterback Ethan Grunkemeyer threw an interception after his pass was tipped a few times. While the defense got another stop, Grunkemeyer was intercepted again on the next drive, this time deep in Stanford territory. The Cardinal then went on a 6-play, 78-yard drive and never looked back.

After the score, Virginia Tech wide receiver Que'Sean Brown was hit and fumbled. Stanford ball again. This time, the Cardinal would start the drive on VT's 29-yard line and scored four plays later. Suddenly, it was 21-0. Lane Stadium was shocked. So was Virginia Tech's sideline.

On their next drive, the Hokies leaned on freshman running back Jeffrey Overton Jr., who didn't disappoint. Overton dominated the drive and scored a touchdown to make it 21-7. Unfortunately, Brent Pry's defense would allow Stanford another field goal before halftime.

Down 24-7, the Hokies opened the second half with the football. It didn't matter. They turned it over on four downs on four plays. After a defensive stop, there was some hope when true freshman wide receiver Davion Brown took a Grunkemeyer throw and raced 69 yards to the end zone for a touchdown, making it 24-14 in the third quarter. Suddenly, there was life in Blacksburg.

Too bad the defense gave it right back, failing to get stops on third and fourth downs. The Cardinal ultimately settled for a field goal, but the Hokies had no answer, punting on their next drive. Stanford responded with another field goal, followed by another Hokies' punt. After that last punt, the Cardinal put the game away with one last touchdown.

A disastrous night from start to finish for Virginia Tech. After last week's blowout loss at SMU, no one expected this follow-up performance. The Hokies were 15.5-point favorites.

Grunkemeyer had a rough night, completing 17 of 34 passes for 270 yards with two touchdowns and two interceptions. He was also sacked five times.

Overton was the star of the show for the Hokies, carrying the ball 19 times for 107 yards and a touchdown. He had no negative runs.

The most important statistic: VT lost the turnover battle 3-0.

A once-promising first year under Franklin has gone off the rails over the last two weeks. And it could be worse with a trip to Miami next week.

The Hokies are now 6-4, and 3-4 in ACC play.

#2778. Rockets fourth-quarter three-point shooting has been clutch

After their first two-game losing streak of the season, where the Houston Rockets suffered losses to the Dallas Mavericks and Phoenix Suns, the Rockets have quickly righted the ship, and after a suprisingly hard fought win over the Utah Jazz, the Rockets have now won three straight and are 10-3 on the season.

Alperen Sengun finished with the second-most points in a game in his career, carrying the Rockets with 43 points. The Rockets relinquished a 12-point lead early in the third quarter as the 1-11 Jazz actually took the lead at one point. The Rockets and Jazz traded blows for most of the third quarter, leading into the fourth.

In the fourth quarter, Sengun continued his dominance, controlling the game. Of course, his play had a lot to do with the Rockets' win, but another area that the Rockets have excelled at all season also played a big part. The Rockets entered the game as the league leaders in fourth-quarter three-point shooting.

The Rockets have been one of the best three-point shooting teams all season, coming into Friday's game ranked seventh overall from downtown at 37.4 percent. Some games are over early when one team dominates the other, and the result is never in doubt, but a lot of games come down to the last few minutes and become back-and-forth contests.

That is why the Rockets' league-leading fourth-quarter three-point shooting is so important. Several times this season, the Rockets have made multiple shots from downtown in a row in the final period, which completely shifts the momentum in a close game.

The Rockets have seen their fourth-quarter three-point shooting improve over the last three seasons. In the 2024-25 season, the Rockets were bottom five in this category; last season, they improved to tenth, and this season, they are the best in the league.

That happened again in Friday's win, as Bogdan Bogdanović and Kevin Durant each hit a huge three-pointer, with the Jazz cutting the lead to one late in the fourth quarter. The Rockets' fourth-quarter shooting matters in close regular-season games, but especially in high-pressure playoff games, and could be the difference between another first-round exit and the Rockets' first deep playoff run since the 2017-18 season.

#2777. Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons' firm has deep ties to the chipmaker

In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC.

The Wall Street firm liked what it heard.

"We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock.

Yet the firm, formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings.

The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China. Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, Axios reported Nov. 11.

By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to a Nov. 10 Axios report, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina.

Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership.

Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5.

An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia.

Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota, said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great."

"His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC.

There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions.

"Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC.

Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick, Brandon Lutnick and Kyle Lutnick did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings.

As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday.

Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary.

But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."

Bessent pointed to Commerce as the department responsible for imposing the entity list, which identifies restricted businesses and other groups, adding, "You will have to ask them about their internal processes."

Nvidia was Cantor's second-largest reported stock position before Howard Lutnick left Wall Street to become commerce secretary in February 2025, behind only bitcoin investor MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy. At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth $479 million, according to its quarterly securities filing.

That share count held steady through September 2025, but its value climbed 36% to $652 million, according to Cantor's quarterly securities filing, as the Trump administration moved over the summer to ease restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China.

Over the following six months, however, the number of Nvidia shares Cantor reported holding fell by 49%, to 3 million in December and 1.78 million by the end of March 2026, with their value dropping from $652 million to $310 million, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings.

Pressure on Howard Lutnick was also mounting on Capitol Hill. Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., in March urged the secretary to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after three people linked to Nvidia customer Super Micro Computer were indicted on charges of conspiring to smuggle AI chips to China.

"The Trump administration, I think, leaks like a sieve when it comes to nonpublic government information getting to various hedge fund guys," Painter said, though he stressed there is no evidence Howard Lutnick had shared such information with his sons.

The filings do not establish why Cantor's reported share count fell or whether its overall financial exposure to Nvidia declined. Nvidia’s stock had more than doubled from its April 2025 lows by late October, before retreating in the following months. The stock fell about 6.5% between the end of September and the end of March.

Cantor's reported Nvidia holdings remained near that lower level through June 30, the latest quarter covered by public disclosures, at 1.81 million shares. Its next quarterly filing is due Monday.

Cantor has not publicly explained the decline.

Most of those shares were attributed to CF Secured, a Cantor brokerage subsidiary that uses stocks and derivatives to hedge customer transactions, according to its audited financial statements. Cantor also disclosed substantial Nvidia options positions during the time period CNBC examined, overwhelmingly skewed toward put options, which can protect against declines in the stock price.

As concerns about Huang escalated inside the Trump administration in May, according to the Nov. 11 Axios report, Cantor was helping finance the expansion of one of Nvidia's newest business partners, securities filings show.

On May 7, Nvidia and Australia-based cloud computing provider IREN announced a five-year, $3.4 billion cloud computing contract and a strategic partnership giving the chipmaker the right to invest up to $2.1 billion in IREN.

"That's not a passive financial investment. Nvidia is a partner who wins as we deliver," IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told investors on the company's quarterly earnings call that day.

Five days later, as Trump headed to China aboard Air Force One, Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned him about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, The New York Times reported Tuesday. Huang, who had not initially been invited on the trip, joined the president's delegation during a refueling stop in Alaska.

Howard Lutnick had already been sent a highly classified intelligence memo detailing concerns about Huang's relationship, according to the Nov. 10 Axios report.

On May 12, the day Trump departed for China, IREN announced the pricing of a convertible bond offering that ultimately raised $3 billion when it closed two days later. Cantor was one of seven bookrunners on the deal, alongside JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs.

On the day the offering closed, May 14, Lutnick's Commerce Department quietly cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies, including Alibaba and ByteDance, to buy Nvidia's advanced H200 chips, though some of those approvals predated the intelligence memo.

It is unclear when IREN hired Cantor for the offering or how much the firm earned from the deal. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.

Cantor reported a substantial position in IREN's stock.

By the end of June, Cantor reported $115 million in IREN shares and $362 million in Nvidia shares. Together, the two companies accounted for more than 9% of the value of Cantor's reported $5.2 billion in securities holdings, excluding options, according to CNBC's analysis of the filing.

IREN was not the only company in Nvidia's orbit that turned to Cantor for financing.

In October 2025, Cantor advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal to support its data center campus in Abilene, Texas, the first site of Stargate, the massive AI infrastructure project backed by OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle.

Newmark, a commercial real estate firm controlled by Cantor, also helped finance the Abilene campus, arranging a $7.1 billion construction loan in May 2025.

Ten months later, Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion for a roughly 20% stake in Lancium, with up to $1 billion more tied to future milestones, The Information reported in August. Lancium, which is also backed by Blackstone, confirmed an investment and a technology partnership on Aug. 24 without disclosing financial terms.

It's unclear whether Cantor continued advising Lancium after the financing deal or played a role in Nvidia's investment. Neither Cantor nor Lancium responded to questions about the investment.

Cantor's reported ties also extend to Nvidia's supply chain.

In May 2025, days after Howard Lutnick announced the transfer of his ownership stake in Cantor to his children via trusts, Semafor reported that bankers at the firm had informally advised executives at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which makes Nvidia's most advanced chips, on navigating Washington. Cantor called Semafor's report "baseless and false."

TSMC received billions of dollars in federal subsidies created during the Biden administration and administered by the Commerce Department to fund its U.S. manufacturing expansion.

Democratic senators called for an ethics investigation in December into whether the Lutnick family stood to benefit from Howard Lutnick's push to expand AI data centers.

And on Wednesday, Sens. Warren and Chris Coons, D-Del., demanded that Howard Lutnick, Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve records on Nvidia's chip exports to China and intelligence warnings about Huang.

The senators questioned whether "prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken or national security recommendations were overruled."

"The place where I think the Trump administration has most failed here is in being persuaded by Jensen Huang and others to license the export of some advanced chips," Coons said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box," accusing the administration of turning a blind eye to the black market for more advanced chips.

#2776. How Rockstar's 'GTA VI' release could reshape gaming, streaming and even paid time off

It's been 13 years since the last installment of Grand Theft Auto, and fans are getting ready for what analysts say could be the biggest video game launch of all time.

The latest game in the franchise, "Grand Theft Auto VI," is set to launch on Nov. 19, after Take-Two Interactive's Rockstar Games delayed its launch twice. Roth analyst Eric Handler estimated the game maker spent more than $1 billion developing the game.

Sales figures could end up breaking records. Sensor Tower estimated over 12 million preorders through Nov. 13, and Morgan Stanley forecast the game could sell 40 million copies by March 2027.

Beyond launch week, the Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, franchise has a track record of lasting engagement over many years. Even 13 years after launch, "Grand Theft Auto V" is one of the top five most viewed games on Twitch this year.

In anticipation of the game's launch, investors have been taking note: Take-two's stock has more than doubled since the beginning of 2023.

The release is seen as not only a monumental moment for developer Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two, but also a massive opportunity for the entire gaming industry.

Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick addressed demand in a recent "Squawk Box" interview, saying, "We tend to be pretty judicious when we talk about this sort of thing, but our expectations were high and they are being vastly exceeded so far."

A creator who goes by the name Deansocool, who has 375,000 followers on Twitch and posts content to YouTube and other social platforms as well, said "GTA VI" will enable creators to grow their audience and provide a massive opportunity for newer streamers to make a name for themselves.

"This game is going to make a lot of millionaires in 2027. A lot of creators gotta understand this is it. This is that golden ticket. This is like a hundred times bigger than Fortnite," he said in an interview with CNBC.

"It goes beyond this launch moment into this sustaining opportunity for them to grow, build, engage and retain their audience and ultimately support themselves by making money," said Twitch Chief Product Officer Mike Minton.

The release of the latest Grand Theft Auto title could draw so much attention that its impact will be felt beyond just the world of gaming.

BambooHR, a workplace time-off platform, reported that paid time off requests for the "GTA VI" release date are nearly 13% higher than equivalent days in 2024 and 2025. It also noted that nearly one in five workers are planning to take time off for the launch.

PwC issued a report examining all the different sectors of the economy that could benefit from the game's launch — or be hurt by it. The firm projected that food delivery companies could see a surge from hunkered-down gamers, and Miami tourism could benefit. PwC noted that foreign visitors to Seoul's Bukchon Hanok Village, which inspired a location in the hit Netflix movie KPop Demon Hunters, increased 118% in the four weeks following the movie's debut.

Music streaming also looks set to get a boost. Tom Petty's "Love Is a Long Road," which appeared in the first "GTA VI" trailer in December 2023, reportedly saw Spotify streams jump by more than 37,000%.

On the downside, the game could distract from movies and streaming entertainment.

"How are people spending Thanksgiving? There's a lot of sports on TV, but you've also got a pretty solid group of your demographics that are going to be focused on playing 'GTA VI,'" said Bart Spiegel, who leads PwC's Global Entertainment & Media sector. "You're going to start to pull eyeballs away from video streaming platforms.

"I think you're going to hear a lot of analyst calls in the first quarter of 2027 saying, 'Hey, listen, some of our numbers were down because of the release of this game,'" Spiegel added.

Rockstar Games declined CNBC's interview request. Watch the video above to learn more.

#2775. 5 key numbers from Iowa football's victory over Purdue

IOWA CITY — The Iowa football team won its third straight game on Nov. 14, beating Purdue 28-7 at Kinnick Stadium.

The Hawkeyes have now won nine in a row under the lights at Kinnick, dating to 2022.

Here are five numbers that tell the story of how the Hawkeyes earned the win.

Iowa's run game was the difference-maker in this game, outrushing the Boilermakers, 246 to 99. Iowa's defense held Purdue to 3.5 average yards per carry, while the Hawkeyes averaged 5.6.

L.J. Phillips led the way with 123 yards on 23 carries, followed by Xavier Williams with 55 on four carries.

One surprising rusher on Saturday: quarterback Hank Brown. He carried 10 times for 32 yards and is seemingly becoming more confident in his running ability after scoring a rushing touchdown two weeks in a row.

Jackson has touchdowns in back-to-back games. Last week he returned a kickoff for a score. Against Purdue he caught the Hawkeyes' longest touchdown pass of the year (44 yards). Jackson caught a pass from Hank Brown on the far left side of the field near the Purdue sideline, broke a tackle, then ran across the field as he picked up a few blocks, entering the right corner of the end zone with five seconds remaining in the first half.

Jackson finished as Iowa's leading receiver, with 61 yards on four catches. He had 55 yards on four carries as a rusher, and picked up 12 yards on a kick return.

Lutmer picked off Purdue QB Ryan Browne in the end zone with about a minute to go in the third quarter. It was his first interception of the year.

Lutmer finished the game as the leading tackler for the Hawkeyes, with 10. He recorded six of them solo.

Iowa's defense is holding opposing offenses to a 44.8% success rate on 3rd or 4th down and 2 yards or less, which is 4th-best in FBS. That stat courtesy of the NBC telecast.

Purdue was 5-of-11 on third down and 0-for-2 on fourth down Saturday.

If you've been following social media, you might know that Australian-born punter Boston Everitt's father had a crazy time trying to get to Iowa City due to the FAA ground stop on Friday. He flew 22 hours from Australia, but got stopped at Denver at the time of the shutdown.

Everitt's dad eventually made it to Iowa City, in a car, 11 hours later.

With how successful the offense was Saturday, it wasn't clear if Everitt would even get on the field. But with 5:21 remaining in the game, the Hawkeyes were forced to punt. Everitt's kick from Purdue's 37-yard line was fair-caught at the 11.

All in all, a successful trip for Mr. Everitt. He got to see his son play, and he enjoyed a Hawkeye victory.

This article originally appeared on Des Moines Register: 5 key numbers from Iowa football's victory over Purdue

#2774. D’Angelo Russell and LaMelo Ball: Darling vs. Discarded

Just a few years ago, the Minnesota Timberwolves made a deal for an enigmatic, polarizing point guard using a first-round pick and a franchise legend (do not disrespect Andrew Wiggins, that's my guy), just as they did in this offseason. The Wolves were universally lambasted for this move, with their trade partner being praised for selling high.

D'Angelo Russell is one of the most reviled Wolves of recent history. Despite a few decent years (or months), his turnovers, early shot-clock off-the-dribble threes, and miserable defense led to a benching in the playoffs against the Memphis Grizzlies for Jordan McLaughlin, and his reputation with the fanbase never really recovered. Maybe it's partly that Russell was the outgoing piece on one of the best trades the Wolves franchise have ever pulled off that made him so infinitely laugh-at-able for fans.

Still, Russell's first few months in a Wolves jersey ahead of the COVID lockdown were like lightning in a bottle. Those same fans who now laugh at him were celebrating what he brought to the team in a season that began with Treveon Graham in the starting lineup.

That feels a lot like Wolves fans clamoring for LaMelo Ball as a second star who brings joy instead of moodiness and moroseness.

But the question then becomes a sad one of whether caution is necessary at a time that is so full of joy. Despite the absence of Anthony Edwards, the Timberwolves are on a five-game win streak on the shoulders of Ball. After multiple years of joyless, winning basketball, the Wolves have their heart back. So is that question even worth asking? Is this piece worth writing?

The obvious answer is no. The big difference in LaMelo Ball and D'Angelo Russell's first 12 games for the Wolves is that Minnesota has gone 9-3 with Ball at the helm, an equal reflection of Russell's 3-9.

And yes, the team around these players was far worse in the 2019-20 season than it is now, but still, Minnesota is winning with one young star point guard leading the charge, when his apparent predecessor couldn't do so.

To add to it, the view of the trade is so vastly different already this season. The Golden State Warriors traded Russell, Omari Spellman, and Jacob Evans III for Andrew Wiggins and a top-3 protected first-round pick, which eventually landed at seventh overall and became Jonathan Kuminga (hey, look at that!). Even within that lightning stretch from Russell, Wiggins was playing incredibly well next to Steph Curry. When the draft lottery arrived a few months later, the Wolves landed Anthony Edwards at first-overall, the Warriors took James Wiseman (which was always a bad choice), and the Charlotte Hornets took Ball.

The Warriors would go on to win a title with Wiggins taking his play to another level as the clear second option on offense and an absolutely rabid rebounder, while Russell was quickly downgraded to the third option for a team that was still bottom-10 in the NBA. That certainly played a part.

But now, Naz Reid is miserable in Charlotte, the first rounder the Wolves sent the Hornets is seven years out and completely out of mind, and Ball is playing his way into an All-Star – dare I say an All-NBA – nod.

The perception is entirely opposite, which means that any step back will hurt so much more. Wolves fans have bought in, they've signed up, they've gone to war for this player and this team in a way they hadn't, because the night-to-night performances are consistent and fun. I mean, honestly, we went so hard at an online NBA analyst that he went on a Wolves podcast, got succinctly disproven, and was successfully converted into a believer.

So why can't I shake the feeling of deja vu, that feeling that maybe the Wolves' new star point guard has what it takes to take the Wolves out of the plateau they've been at, one that was eventually only half paid off with Russell.

Ball has been more than a dream outcome so far this season. Reid, as beloved as he was, was always a low price to pay for the guy who was bringing Moussa Diabate into Amare Stoudemire conversations in the context of the Hornets playing to the statistical level of the Run-and-Gun Phoenix Suns. Minnesota got a 6'7 orchestrator and offensive maestro for pennies on the dollar, which is not what they gave up for Russell.

I guess the answer is the same one that I came to in 2020, when Minnesota finished with one of the worst records in the league. While stuck in lockdown, longing for some Wolves basketball, I would hang around and watch the same "Track the Pack" episode welcoming Russell to Minnesota, followed by highlight after highlight of the Malik Beasley, D'Angelo Russell, and Jarred Vanderbilt Wolves.

I chose to enjoy it then. I choose to enjoy this now.

Hopefully, this version of Ball is more real than those first 12 games of Russell were. Hopefully, Minnesota keeps winning behind their point guard of the future. Hopefully, Anthony Edwards returns to an offensive ecosystem that has survived without him, but reaches a new level with him.

But, in the meantime, let's enjoy the team that exists, and remember that comparisons and contrasts do not always come from a place of sad disrespect. Let's enjoy this, Wolves fans. Fun doesn't always last, but it's certainly better now than it has been in years.

Maybe, just maybe, the most fun since that 12-game stretch where Minnesota and fans were sure they had found their joy in D'Angelo Russell.

#2772. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

Democrats' midterm election win has put the artificial intelligence trade in question, as voters clearly expressed opposition to the rapid buildout of data centers. The stock market could remain volatile amid AI trade concerns, macro uncertainties, and geopolitical tensions.

In this scenario, investors can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios to earn steady income. However, the extensive universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as these experts assign ratings after in-depth financial analysis.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Viper Energy (VNOM) is a subsidiary of Diamondback and owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests, primarily in the Permian Basin. The company reported upbeat third-quarter earnings, supported by recent acquisitions and continued development activity from Diamondback and third-party operators. Viper announced a base cash dividend of 50 cents per share for Q3 2026, payable on Nov. 19. Based on the base and variable dividends announced over the past 12 months, VNOM's dividend yield stands at 5.7%.

Following the Q3 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper Energy stock with a price target of $61. The analyst noted that the company delivered solid Q3 results, with production, including oil and natural gas liquids, exceeding both TD Cowen and consensus estimates.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that the key update was the announcement of two royalty acquisitions for $809 million in cash, including deferred consideration, and $82 million of newly issued shares.

Given the recently announced base dividend hike, Bilkoski expects Viper to direct incremental free cash flow toward buybacks. While the acquisitions increase leverage, the analyst believes that Viper has enough capacity for opportunistic buybacks.

Bilkoski noted that Viper has historically delivered one of the highest production per share growth profiles in his royalty coverage, but still trades at a notable discount to the royalty peer average and the company's historical FCF yield range. "In our view, its above-average growth warrants a higher valuation," said the analyst.

Bilkoski ranks No. 525 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.80%. See Viper Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Exxon Mobil (XOM) reported robust Q3 2026 profits, as its U.S. refineries boosted production to capitalize on the high diesel fuel prices sparked by the conflict in the Middle East. The oil and gas giant announced a quarterly dividend of $1.07 per share, payable on Dec. 10, reflecting a 3.9% increase. This marks Exxon's 44th consecutive year of dividend increases. At an annualized dividend of $4.28 per share, XOM offers a yield of 2.53%.

Impressed by the Q3 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Exxon stock and raised his price target to $193 from $180 to reflect higher downstream earnings, with the expectation of increased mid-cycle margins.

Gabelman noted that the strength in Exxon's refining business continues to offset Middle East-related headwinds. He added that the company increased its ownership in LNG projects, which should reduce its Middle East concentration over time from 75% to 50% and lower the likelihood of diversification-focused mergers and acquisitions. Beyond LNG, Gabelman expects Exxon's growth in the 2030s to come from Guyana, Kashagan, Permian, and possibly Venezuela.

Gabelman noted that Exxon announced a dividend hike of nearly 4% and plans to maintain buybacks at $20 billion for 2027. "The decision to maintain reduces the pro-cyclicality nature of the buyback," said the analyst.

Gabelman ranks No. 347 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 66% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.90%. See Exxon Mobil Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Williams (WMB), which owns and operates energy infrastructure to deliver natural gas, reported strong third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of $0.525 per share, or $2.10 per share annualized, payable on Dec. 28. WMB offers a dividend yield of 3.09%.

In reaction to the Q3 2026 results, CIBC analyst Robert Catellier reaffirmed a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $82. The analyst noted that Q3 results were essentially in line with expectations and reflected continued strength in execution across WMB's infrastructure portfolio.

Catellier said that Williams' Q3 performance was driven by higher transmission, storage, and power generation revenues, as well as contributions from the Momentum Midstream acquisition.

He noted that Williams maintained its full-year EBITDA guidance of $8.3 billion to $8.5 billion. #2771. SpaceX catches upper stage of Starship rocket in historic first

After a booster explosion on Friday, SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage, or spacecraft, portion of its massive Starship rocket from orbit on Saturday — a triumphant milestone for the company.

SpaceX made the historic catch using its "chopsticks," mechanical arms attached to a launch tower, at its facility in Starbase, Texas.

Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship test yet, marked the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the rocket's booster and upper stage.

Musk posted a video on X inspecting the upper stage craft after completing the capture.

During the first phase of the test flight on Friday, SpaceX failed to catch and recover the booster, instead diverting it to an offshore splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded before hitting the water.

The rocket's upper stage then continued into orbit and flew around the Earth 14 times before successfully landing on SpaceX's launch tower, nicknamed Mechazilla.

The Hawaii Department of Transportation issued a temporary pause on some West Coast flights Friday, due to debris risk from the flight. Separately, the FAA issued a rare, nationwide ground stop due to telecommunications system failures. (Both of those orders have since been lifted.)

Making Starship a reliable and fully reusable rocket is critical to SpaceX's ambitions. In the near term, the company needs Starship to send more satellites into orbit to expand its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center.

SpaceX is also expected to use Starship to bring astronauts and cargo from lunar orbit to the Moon's surface and back for NASA. Musk also has a grand vision to use Starship to "colonize Mars" and "make humanity multi-planetary."

During Test Flight 15 on Friday, SpaceX released another 26 of its newest Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, growing its commercial satellite internet network.

The company's constellation already included over 11,000 satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket can carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites, the company has said.

#2770. UFC 334 live results, highlights, play-by-play | Gane vs. Hokit

Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) is live TONIGHT (Sat., Nov. 14, 2026) with UFC 334, taking place inside the famous Madison Square Garden in New York City, NY, streaming exclusively live on Paramount+. UFC 334's main event is a big one: Ciryl Gane vs. Josh Hokit is the featured attraction for UFC's Heavyweight crown. The co-main is a big deal, too, with Kayla Harrison vs. Amanda Nunes for UFC's women's Bantamweight belt.

The Josh Hokit experiment reaches its zenith tonight (heaven help us all) with his chance to take UFC's most valuable title from Ciryl Gane. Hokit is only 4-0 in UFC, but his wild brawl with Curtis Blaydes coupled with his demolition of Derrick Lewis on the White House lawn have landed him in MSG. The lack of depth at Heavyweight (and fresh match-ups), along with Hokit's odious persona, have also contributed to this moment.

Gane won the interim title after drubbing Alex Pereira at UFC White House. That title became legit when Tom Aspinall vacated his belt because of long-standing eye issue caused by Gane (knuckle deep!). Gane will attempt to defend a UFC belt for the first time in his career here and prove he's a deserving champ (and not just a dirty fighter).

There's history on the line in the co-main event with Amanda Nunes trying to replicate Georges St-Pierre, in stepping away from the sport at their peak and then returning a few years later and proving they are still the gold standard. Her American Top Team teammate, Kayla Harrison, will try and stop that. Harrison will be trying to show that, despite her lack of exposure in UFC, she deserves to be in the G.W.O.A.T. conversation.

Rounding out this particularly stacked main card is Caio Borralho vs. Yousri Belgaraoui, Uros Medic vs. Kevin Holland, and Bilal Hasan vs. Luis Gurule.
