Round 3: Borralho gets a double leg takedown by the fence. Belgaroui works to his feet, but Borralho is still on him. Belgaroui goes for a guillotine and Borralho bursts out of there. Belgaroui lands a big knee to the body, both guys are very tired right now. Belgaroui brings the knee upstairs. Barralho lands a big punch. Borralho lands another big double leg, with a minute left on the clock.

Official decision: Caio Borralho def. Yousri Belgaroui by unanimous decision (30-27, 30-27, 30-27)

Round 1: Medic lands a punch of Holland's shoulder and then goes for a high kick. He misses and hits the deck. He gets up quickly and Holland is talking to him. Holland throws up some front kicks. Medic comes in and cracks him with a left hook. Holland pumps his jab and flaps his gums again. Medic falls on another kick attempt. Holland lands an uppercut shortly after. Holland leans out the way of a Medic straight and then fires back, knocking Medic down. Medic gets up, but Holland throws him down and then jumps on his neck. He goes for a guillotine, but then switches it to a D'arce. He takes Medic down and there's a minute left. Medic is able to gut it out, but Holland gets it again as Medic tries to stand. Medic is again holding on and is able to get out of it.

Round 2: Holland catches a kick to the cup. Holland takes about a minute before saying he's good to go. He's smiling and talking to Medic. Not a lot of action here, just single shots and nothing landing hard. Medic gets close and throws a combo, but Holland is able to block most of it. Holland blocks a head kick. They get close and Medic lands another kick to the cup. This time Holland takes his sweet time. Marc Goddard deducts a point from Medic and we're back on. Holland goes for a takedown, gets on Medic's back, Medic rolls and somehow ends up standing again. Holland grabs him and puts him on the fence.

Round 3: Medic catches Holland with a short counter. Holland wraps him up, possibly to get some recovery time. Holland puts Medic on the fence. He uses some knees and shoulder strikes. Medic is finding Holland's size really tough to deal with the in the clinch. Goddard breaks the clinch. They trade body kicks. Medic lands some nice shots again, but Holland is able to roll with them. Medic lands another good shot, a straight left. But Holland is able to slide back as it lands. Holland level changes right into a kick attempt and gets a shin right on his ear. He's wobbled, but Medic is very hesitant. medic tries to get the finish, but there's not enough time.

Official decision: Kevin Holland vs. Uros Medic ends in a majority draw (29-27, 28-28, 28-28)

Round 1: Hasan flashes high kicks early on, his speed is incredible. Gurule stays contained and is patiently trying to walk him down. Gurule gets close and lands a punch, but Hasan pushes him off and gets him back to kicking range. Hasan whiffs on some spin kicks. He lands a front kick to the body. Gurule blocks a switch kick and then lands a right hook that drops Hasan! Hasan bounces up again and seems fine. Gurule landed the best shot, but Hasan controlled the rest of the round. I feel a little dirty doing it, but…

Round 2: Gurule gets close enough to clinch. Hasan lands some nice knees to the body. Gurule gets him to the fence and level changes. He can't complete the takedown, though. Hasan gets back into space. Hasan lands a nice spinning kick to the body. Gurule has landed a few inside leg kicks. He's looking for that right hook again, though. Gurule ducks down and gets a double leg takedown on the fence. Gurule lands some elbows from Hasan's full guard.

Round 3: Gurule lands a short right and then transitions right to a takedown. Gurule is split open, somehow. Hasan caught him with a short elbow on the takedown. Gurule is in Hasan's half guard. Gurule lands hammerfists, desperate to avoid a stand up. Gurule has Hasan stuck to the ground, with his shoulder pressure and also his toes in the fence (which the referee is totally blind to). Gurule is beating him up.

Official decision: Luis Gurule def. Bilal Hasan by split decision (28-29, 29-28, 29-28)

Stephen Thompson vs. Charles Radtke: Wonderboy gets his walk-off moment! Radtke seemed like he had a chance to out-wrestle Thompson in the first round. He got tired quickly, though. In the second round Thompson was able to get into a groove and started to chip away with solid single shots. He almost finished Radtke at the end of the second. In the third he put him away with a spinning heel kick, making maybe the best highlight of his career.

Official decision: Stephen Thompson def. Charles Radtke by KO (spinning hook kick), round 3 (2:54)

Drew Dober vs. Chris Duncan: Duncan kept Dober at leg's length for the first two rounds with constant head and body kicks. Dober blocked most, but they succeeded in preventing Dober from blitzing forwards and starting a war. In the third round Duncan slowed down and Dober tried to get a finish, but after hurting Duncan late he gave up a takedown and Duncan was able to ride out the fight in top position.

Official decision: Chris Duncan def. Drew Dober by unanimous decision (30-27, 30-27. 29-28)

Jim Miller vs. Terrance McKinney: McKinney got to work quickly, of course. He hurt Miller with his jab, ripped a kick to the body and then landed a flush left on the chin that put Miller down. McKinney pounced with ground and pound for the win. Miller was able to tag McKinney with some counters, but he didn't have the power to stop McKinney doing what he does best.

Official decision: Terrance McKinney def. Jim Miller by KO (punches), round 1 (1:53)

Cesar Almeida vs. Donte Johnson: Johnson was very aggressive in this fight, winging punches at Almeida. They mostly found his shoulders and forearms, though. After blocking all that, Almeida landed right on the button, with a perfect straight punch, and dropped Johnson. Johnson survived the follow ups and got back to his feet. Johnson tried to fight fire with fire, but Almeida was able to sting Johnson again and again until the ref had seen enough.

Official decision: Cesar Almeida def. Donte Johnson by TKO (punches), round 1 (3:20)

Melquizael Costa vs. Jared Gordon: Costa lit up Gordon with kicks from all directions in the first. In the second he ended up on the bottom and then threatened Gordon with a deep triangle attempt. Gordon survived and Costa seemed to gas out from the effort. Still, Costa did enough to survive and bank the decision victory.

Official decision: Melquizael Costa def. Jared Gordon by unanimous decision (29-28, 29-28, 29-28)

Bia Mesquita vs. Macy Chiasson: Total domination from Mesquita. She got a body lock takedown and then toyed with Chiasson on the ground. She hurt her with ground and pound, flattened her out and then put the rear naked choke in for yet another submission win. Look out Kayla/Amanda.

Official decision: Bia Mesquita def. Macy Chiasson by submission (rear naked choke), round 1 (3:22)

Juan Diaz vs. Alatengheili: Diaz had so much success boxing with Alatengheili that he didn't need to use his grappling. He just kept clubbing the Alatengheili with two shot combos, landing quick and slipping out before he get receive any payback. He basically tripled up Alatengheili on sig. strikes. The only thing that cost him a finish was how tough Alatengheili proved to be.

Official decision: Juan Diaz def. Alatengheili by unanimous decision (30-27, 30-27, 30-27)

Evan Elder vs. Samuel Sanches: Elder hurt Sanches early in the fight and also showed off a superior ground game. The youngster Sanches showed some nice striking in return, though. He wobbled Elder and also caused a massive cut. For all the good things Sanches did, though, Elder did more — in each round. Sanches was also deducted a point for fence grabbing.

Official decision: Evan Elder def. Samuel Sanches by unanimous decision (30-26, 30-26, 30-26)

#2769. Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors

Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang."

Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker.

Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing, with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June.

The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress, who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence.

"But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed. The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China.

SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees.

Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost."

Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee.

Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify.

The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times.

President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping, according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

#2768. The 2nd quarter of Texans vs. Chargers cost safety Jalen Pitre $30k

Jalen Pitre was hit with not one, but two big fines for his play against the Chargers in Week 9. Pitre owes the league $30,800 for unnecessary roughness/use of the helmet on two separate plays.

Both plays occurred in the second quarter of the Texans' 44-22 win over the worst team in the NFL right now. On the first, at 8:58, Pitre's fine for use of the helmet came on a tackle of Chargers WR Tre Harris on third-and-goal for a 7-yard loss. The play forced the Chargers to settle for a field goal.

The second play, with :25 left in the first half, was a tackle on Chargers TE Charlie Kolar for a 5-yard game. Pitre was not flagged for either play during the game.

Pitre has been fined three previous times in his NFL career for a total of $43,351, and the two fines from Texans vs. Chargers are his first since Jan. 2024.

On the Chargers side, cornerback Donte Jackson was fined $12,537 for unnecessary roughness/striking, kicking, or kneeing for a play in the fourth quarter of Texans vs. Chargers, a Woody Marks carry for no gain. Jackson was flagged for the infraction at the time.

The NFL divides the money it collects from player discipline and splits it between the NFLPA's efforts to support retired players, the NFL Foundation, and other nonprofits that support sports leagues, community wellness, and player health and safety initiatives at every level of sports.

#2767. Game Preview: Nets close out the road trip in Memphis

The Brooklyn Nets saw what "worse" looked like on Wednesday night against the New Orleans Pelicans. Brooklyn certainly has its issues, but they pale in comparison to the nightmare New Orleans fans have to sit through right now. The Nets cruised to a 145-111 blowout victory. Yeesh.

Tonight's opponent, however, has been one of the pleasant surprises of the 2026-27 NBA season. The Memphis Grizzlies enter Saturday at 8-4 and in great shape — though, much like Brooklyn, they just beat the stuffing out of those same Pelicans, rolling to a 142-111 win last night. My goodness.

Matchup: Brooklyn Nets (3-8) at Memphis Grizzlies (8-4)

PROBABLE — Nolan Traore (right calf soreness/tightness)

QUESTIONABLE — Michael Porter Jr. (personal reasons)

OUT – Joshua Jefferson (G League Assignment)

OUT – Tyler Bilodeau (G League – Two-Way)

OUT – Zach Edey (left ankle injury management)

OUT – Scotty Pippen Jr (lumbar disc herniation)

OUT – Richie Saunders (right knee surgery)

This is night two of a back-to-back for the Grizzlies. However, nobody played over 30 minutes last night so theoretically everyone should be good to go. We'll see.

Grizzlies head coach Tuomas Iisalo has this offense humming this season, and this breakdown by Adam Pike dives into some of his favorite actions. He's earned complete buy-in from this young roster, and the early results have been promising so far.

Memphis' most promising cornerstone is someone the franchise hopes carries them into the next generation. Rookie Cameron Boozer adjusted to the NBA seamlessly and somehow still has plenty of room to grow. He's second among rookies in assists per game, a pretty impressive feat for a power forward, alongside 9.8 rebounds a night. And watching Boozer also makes me realize I watched his dad's journey from college at Duke all the way to the pros and beyond. Time flies, man.

Boozer will draw plenty of Julius Randle. After Wednesday's win, Randle praised the organization and structure of Brooklyn's offense. It also helped that they only committed 15 turnovers as a team, their second lowest amount this season. When you actually get shots up at the rim, good things tend to happen.

Brooklyn will need a big night out of Day'ron Sharpe to steal a road win. Memphis is third in the NBA in rebounding (47.9 RPG) this season, and Sharpe is still Brooklyn's best weapon on the glass. Sharpe has been steady this year and the Nets are going to need him to hold Boozer, Isaiah Stewart, and the rest of the Grizzlies' frontcourt off the offensive boards.

There are two schools of thought related to Egor Demin. One is to praise for maintaining good three-point percentages while taking a high volume of threes when he's on the court. That success can carry him a long way and guarantee he's always on the court. The other is to express worry that he hasn't been getting to the rim at rates that make the defense worry about him inside the arc.

As of this writing, he's averaging six drives to the rim per game and his frequency of shots at the rim is greater than what it was last year. However, it's only seven shots at the rim so you can't read that much into it.

Demin is going to have to add more to his game if he wants to reach that next level. And we'll see if tonight's the night Demin and Mikel Brown Jr get real minutes on the court tonight.

MBJ is listed as questionable, so we'll see if he's back out there. It's been a frustrating experience for a lot of Nets fans, and it's understandable. This team has to figure out what their future is and fast, and that comes with getting your youngsters real minutes together so you can properly evaluate what's working and what's not.

It's always fun watching a player's steady ascent pay off. Ty Jerome has been an analytics-crowd favorite for the past couple of seasons, and this year he's putting it all together. He's averaging a career high 25.4 points and 5.3 assists per game and is outpacing other franchise cornerstones such as Cade Cunningham and Nikola Jokic.

Even as the Griz kids gain more experience, Jerome will be essential to their growth remains the engine making it work. From Maxwell Ogden at Beale Street Bears:

"As a proven sharpshooter and shot creator, Jerome can play with just about any combination of his teammates. He's just as lethal when working off of scorers and playmakers as he is when he creates his own shots. Furthermore, his mere presence on the court means defenses have to relax the attention they give to the less experienced Grizzlies players."

I'm a sucker for rewarding career role players with All-Star appearances when they're having career years, so I'm hoping Jerome gets the nod this winter.

#2766. Spanish Club Wishes to Sell Player; Olympiacos Skeptical

According to a report by media outlet Sport FM, via TransferFeed, La Liga side Sevilla are aiming to sell Swiss winger Rubén Vargas, with Olympiacos being the club's preferred destination for the player. However, the news also suggested that the Piraeus are no longer engaging with the player's environment, as they no longer wish to bring a winger into their fold.

An earlier report by media outlet Gazzetta.gr, however, said that Olympiacos were interested in signing the Swiss player. That report also said the Red and Whites had shown interest in the player before, including during the last summer window. However, a deal could not materialise then, and Vargas remained in Spain.

The Gazzetta.gr report confirmed an earlier update from media outlet AS via TransferFeed. That report stated that Olympiacos had shown genuine interest in the 28-year-old, with several approaches made to Nervión. However, an agreement could not be reached as the offer made by the Greek club was significantly lower than what Sevilla demanded for the player, which was in the range of 15-20 million euros. AS said, "...several approaches were made to Nervión after Rubén Vargas performed well with Switzerland at the World Cup, and Olympiacos negotiated for his transfer to Athens for many days. The offer from Olympiacos was significantly lower than the 15 to 20 million euros that Sevilla wanted. Neither Sevilla nor the player were convinced by Olympiacos."

A graduate of the academy of Swiss club Luzern, Vargas played 50 league games for the senior squad of the club after making his debut for them in 2017. He left Luzern after two seasons and joined German side FC Augsburg, where he played for six years. During this time, he appeared in 154 official league fixtures and scored 20 goals.

In 2025, Vargas left Germany and arrived in Spain to play for Sevilla. Since joining the Rojiblancos, the winger has played 35 league games and scored 5 goals.

In addition to his club career, the winger has also made 67 official appearances for the senior squad of the Switzerland National Football Team, after playing for their U-20 and U-21 squads. He has scored 13 times for the Rossocrociati.

Whether Olympiacos renews their interest in the player is a question that the future will provide an answer to. However, as things stand, it seems as if the Greek ship has passed for the Swiss winger, and Rubén Vargas may have to look for another club if he indeed has to leave the Estadio Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán.

#2765. Nationwide ground stop followed contractor upgrade to L3Harris telecommunication system: DOT’s Duffy

The longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 came after updates to a telecommunications system managed by contractor L3Harris Technologies, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday, as hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded by lingering disruptions.

There was "zero evidence" that the problem was caused by something "nefarious" or anything related to artificial intelligence, Bryan Bedford, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration, said at a press conference with Duffy.

The upgrades at "at least" one remote location were part of ongoing work of switching from a copper wire system to fiber, Duffy said.

A router had "flooded" other routers in the air traffic control system with over 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, the secretary said, creating problems with airplane communications and radar feeds.

The outage again thrust aging infrastructure that underpins U.S. air traffic control into the spotlight, along with the country's struggles to replace sections of it while operating the world's busiest airspace.

"What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router," he said.

L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel."

L3Harris said it has completed more than 70% of the switch from copper wiring to fiber-optic system.

Duffy took the groundstop to seek billions more from lawmakers to modernize the system.

Bedford said no FAA facilities went dark but that officials decided to ground flights because of "instability" in information feeds to air traffic control centers that handle en route aircraft at high altitudes and eventually to others closer to airports.

"We were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a center losing connectivity with aircraft," said Bedford. He said officials weren't sure for about 45 minutes what was causing the instability.

Flight disruptions continued on Saturday. Nearly 6,500 U.S. flights were canceled Saturday and more than 8,000 were delayed as of 9 p.m. ET, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. That's on top of more than 9,000 U.S. flight cancellations, about a third of the day's schedule, and more than 7,000 delays on Friday, though some disruptions were due to bad weather.

Friday had the second-highest U.S. flight cancellations since a severe blizzard and below-freezing temperatures in January, according to aviation-data firm Cirium.

Part of untangling from the ground stop includes getting aircraft where they need to be. The ground stop forced many planes to divert to other airports, while dozens of planes had to park with limited gate space because flights couldn't depart.

Airlines run one of the lightest schedules on Saturday and are deploying as many spare planes and crews as possible to get travelers and employees where they need to be as they're eager to start fresh for the upcoming Thanksgiving holiday period.

American Airlines, for example, is offering flight attendants extra pay to pick up trips, according to a person familiar with the airline's plans.

Delta Air Lines offered crews double pay to pick up trips and gave them confirmed seats on flights to get them into position, according to internal company messages CNBC saw. United Airlines was also offering pilots and flight attendants extra pay to pick up flights through Sunday, according to people familiar with the matter.

American, along with other airlines, said it would change customers' tickets at no fee or fare difference if the outage affected their plans and that it would cap some airfares.

Around 3 million people were scheduled to fly on Saturday, according to Cirium.

The FAA had halted departing U.S. flights around 4 p.m. ET on Friday, a ground stop that lasted more than four hours, the longest such pause on departing flights in 25 years.

Duffy on Friday blamed outdated U.S. infrastructure for the problem and said Congress needs to approve more money to overhaul the country's air traffic control. Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have angered airline executives for years, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

It was the second time the FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks. Trump administration officials have repeatedly said it did not appear to be a cyberattack.

The U.S. has the world's busiest airspace.

"Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," the FAA said late Friday.

The disruption also upended travel for NBA, NHL and college teams, which struggled to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend.

Duffy said college football teams traveling on charter flights could receive priority.

"I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they have games going off tomorrow," he said during a Friday press briefing.

The Southeastern Conference announced on X that some games had been moved to Sunday due to the flight disruption.

"We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses," the SEC said in a statement shared on X.

The National Football League said that it is putting in three backup referees for three games on Sunday because of the ground stop, "reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns."

— CNBC's April Roach and Jessica Golden contributed to this article.

#2764. Bills trending up, trending down: The players who will decide game at Jets

The Bills lead the NFL in points per game (32.0) and total yards per game (386.4), and they head to MetLife at 7-1 on a four-game winning streak. The Jets are 2-7 and have lost four in a row, which makes this look like a game that plays itself. Joe Brady spent the week telling reporters that records can mislead in this league, and New York gives him some material: the NFL's fifth-highest pressure rate (39.2 percent), 22 sacks, and a rookie in David Bailey, the second overall pick, who is tied for fourth in sacks (7.5) and tied for the league lead in forced fumbles (five). (Spencer Brown, Buffalo's starting right tackle, is doubtful with an ankle injury.)

Buffalo's last two wins, 36-10 over the Ravens and 23-6 in Minnesota, were its two biggest of the season, and the defense gave up 16 points across both. That unit had allowed 29 or more points in five of its first six games, so the last two weeks matter. The question mark is the quarterback list: Carson Wentz, and a Ravens group that got one pass from Lamar Jackson. Geno Smith isn't a world beater by any means, but he is an experienced starting QB in this league, with some real young talent around him. If they're allowed to get hot and enjoy the game, it can turn into a tough afternoon for Buffalo very quickly.

Without further ado, here are the players I believe will need to be at their best so the Bills can earn their eighth win of the season:

James Cook carried 31 times for 107 yards and a touchdown in Minneapolis, 10 more carries than any other running back in Week 9. He averaged 2.7 yards per carry through three quarters behind Tylan Grable and Austin Corbett on the left side, then the Vikings' front wore down: 47 yards on one fourth-quarter possession that ended with his five-yard touchdown, and Buffalo held the ball for 42:32 to Minnesota's 17:28. PFF still graded him 52.9, a reminder that the yardage came on volume more than clean running.

The Jets are the kind of defense volume works against. They rank 26th against the run at 128.0 yards per game, and it is getting worse: about 118 per game through five weeks, just over 140 over the last four. Kansas City ran for 163 yards at 5.1 yards per carry last Sunday. The advanced numbers disagree on the details, so I'll flag it: the Jets are ninth in EPA per rush allowed (-0.142), which strips out garbage time, yet 30th in rush success rate allowed (51.5 percent). That reads to me like a defense that gives up steady, unspectacular gains, and those add up late.

On the other hand, Cook is fifth in the NFL with 814 rushing yards, tied for eighth at 4.8 per carry, and he has scored in seven straight games. Since 2021, the Jets have allowed the Bills 145 rushing yards per game, 4.6 per carry, and 15 touchdowns across ten meetings, per the Jets' own site. The one thing that can interrupt this is the football itself. That same site notes Cook has fumbled ten times since the start of last season (I flagged it in Week 6), and Bailey's five forced fumbles lead the league. If Cook holds on to it, I expect a 25-carry day that gets better as it goes.

Ed Oliver has played five games this season, and the defense looks different with him in them. Through the first stretch, Buffalo allowed 25.3 points per game with him on the field and 31.7 without; in the two games since his return, it allowed 10 and 6. In Minneapolis, he played 28 snaps (58 percent), had three quarterback hits and graded 79.1 at PFF, the fifth-best mark on the defense. A PFF-based breakdown from The IDP Show has him at 11 pressures over those two games with no sacks and a 72.1 pass-rush grade for the season.

Oliver has been around for a while now, but something has changed — Deone Walker, the nose tackle, was double-teamed on 71 percent of defensive snaps while Oliver was out, and he has earned the attention with an 86.1 PFF pass-rush grade (second among 126 qualifying interior linemen), 25 pressures and a spot on PFF's midseason All-Pro second team. His run-defense grade is 61.9, 41st at the position, but the eye test certainly gives me some "he's been better than this" vibes. With Breece Hall back from his quadriceps injury (15 carries for 61 yards last week) and Braelon Allen fourth in the league in rushing yards over expected (+124) and sixth at 5.0 per carry, I expect the Walker-Oliver combo to be at their best on Sunday.

Spencer Brown did not practice Thursday or Friday and is doubtful. I expect Grable at right tackle, with Dawkins back at left tackle and Anderson at left guard; Dawkins (ribs) and Anderson (ankle) both practiced fully on Friday and carry no designation. Right has been his best side. Before Minneapolis, most of his work had come there, including 82 snaps against Baltimore in his first real start, where charting-based metrics hit him with two pressures on 42 pass-blocking snaps, both in true pass sets. Against the Vikings, he moved to left tackle for all 80 snaps, and PFF graded him 51.0 overall with a 40.2 pass-blocking grade and four pressures allowed. PFF had him at 55.8 for the season over 133 snaps before that game.

Bailey is the problem, though. He has 40 pressures on 194 rushes (20.6 percent, second-highest among players with at least 100), plus the sacks and the forced fumbles. PFF is less impressed by how he wins: a 10.3 percent pass-rush win rate (56th of 91 edge rushers) and a 66.0 pass-rush grade (38th). That gap suggests a rusher who finishes plays and benefits from the pressure around him more than one who beats tackles clean every snap, which is a matchup a swing tackle can survive. Brady said the Jets move Bailey around the formation, so it could be more about quickly recognizing stunt games and where the pressure is coming from, than simply neutralizing the man lining up in front of you. Allen was sacked four times in Minneapolis, and the bar for Grable is keeping Bailey from ending drives: no sacks, and no strips that reach the ball.

The Bills sent a 2027 second-round pick to Tennessee on Tuesday for Amani Hooker and a fifth, after releasing C.J. Gardner-Johnson, and Hooker said Wednesday he would play Sunday. He arrives with five interceptions, tied for the NFL lead and the most of any safety, three of them against Joe Burrow in Week 8. PFF has him at 81.0 overall, 75.2 in coverage (10th among 100 safeties) and 83.9 against the run (10th), and he played 99 percent of the Titans' snaps across seven games. Buffalo's defense had six interceptions through eight games and allowed 238.8 passing yards per game, the fourth-most in the league, with 28 completions of 20-plus yards.

He doesn't need to be the savior, though. The timing helps. The defense has allowed 10 and 6 points in its last two games, with six sacks over two weeks, and a new safety fits more easily on a unit that is already playing fast. Cole Bishop played all 48 snaps in Minneapolis, Damar Hamlin played 44, and Geno Stone 25, so the first thing to watch is who gives up snaps to Hooker. The test is Garrett Wilson, who leads the Jets with 527 yards and three touchdowns and practiced fully on Friday after a concussion, plus rookie Omar Cooper Jr. (306 yards and two touchdowns in five games, with an 83.3 percent catch rate. Jim Leonhard said the Jets create clean pictures for Smith and get the ball out. A safety with Hooker's range and run-defense grade is supposed to muddy those pictures and shrink the explosive plays, and if he does it in his first game, the case for the trade makes itself.

Connor McGovern, C: PFF graded him 75.5 in Minneapolis, fourth-best on the offense, with Dion Dawkins and Alec Anderson both out against the league's heaviest-blitzing defense. The Jets rank fifth in pressure rate, and McGovern was limited Wednesday and Thursday with a neck injury before a full practice Friday and no designation.

Ty Johnson, RB: Johnson played only 17 snaps (21 percent) and still graded 79.0, third-best on the offense, with a 36-yard catch on a third down early in the third quarter. He has 17 catches for 210 yards in six games, and against a defense that sends extra rushers, he should have more opportunities to produce.

Khalil Shakir, WR: Shakir caught all four of his targets for 58 yards (PFF: 80.1, second-best on the offense). Over his last five games, he has 23 catches on 27 targets for 318 yards. The Jets lean on man coverage, and Shakir is Josh Allen's quick answer when the rush arrives.

Dorian Williams, LB: Williams played just 19 snaps (40 percent, down from 29 a week earlier) and graded 92.8, second on the defense behind Terrel Bernard's 94.9. His interception came with T.J. Hockenson covered one-on-one down the seam, his second of the season after the one against the Raiders in Week 6. I had him in a different corner of this list for coverage that week, so the play stood out. The Jets use four tight ends (Kenyon Sadiq, Mason Taylor, Jeremy Ruckert and Jelani Woods), and that is his test.

Aaron Glenn is 0-8 against AFC East opponents as Jets head coach, and Brady is right that New York has played in plenty of one-score games. I'd like to see a more pass-happy approach built on Allen's playmaking ability, like in the first couple of games. It could result in a blowout win, with the Jets struggling to keep up with the most prolific offense in the league. However, that approach got Allen banged up real quick, so I expect Brady to keep riding Cook and the run game until the Jets really force Superman to put the cape on. On defense, Oliver and Walker will have to squeeze the pocket, and Hooker can make an impact on the safety group for the first time. The risk sits on a talented divisional rival, playing at home, putting together a strong game against the AFC leaders who could overlook them.

Which worries you more on Sunday: Grable against Bailey, or something else? Tell me in the comments!

#2762. Film study: What is the Wizards’ offense missing?

Before Thursday night's barnburner of a loss to the Pistons in double overtime, the vibes around the Wizards, and their offense in particular, were nearing a free fall. The Wiz have the league's 26th-ranked offense, even after the onslaught against Detroit.

There were, to be sure, positive signals to glean. Alex Sarr played by far his best game of the season, knocking down four threes. Trae Young showed more scoring juice, shooting 17 free throws and hitting a buzzer-beater to force OT. Sarr and Anthony Davis connected on a rare lob in overtime.

But the underlying issues behind the bricktastic 4-9 start will take longer to solve. The Wizards barely shoot any threes, and miss most of the ones they do try. Only the Bulls have shot a worse percentage from deep so far. With poor spacing and clumsy jumbo lineups, the offense has tilted concerningly toward true Trae Young heliocentrism; Young leads the league in seconds per touch.

The Wizards use core actions that make a fair amount of sense for their personnel. They rely on side-to-side movement, hoping to launch Young downhill and create better angles for the pick and roll. Consider this frequent action, with Kyshawn George maneuvering to the wing (pending the much-awaited return of NBA.com's video clips, I'm using screenshots for now):

That's an Iverson cut, intended to distract the defense and free up a Young-AD pick and roll. When Young starts going downhill, Tre Johnson flies up in tandem from the opposite corner. But the Pacers easily box Young toward the wing and funnel the ball away from the middle:

Young makes the pass to AJ Dybantsa, but Pascal Siakam closes him down, and Dybantsa, with no advantage, throws the ball away. This is not an uncommon sight for the Wizards — a Young pick and roll in tight confines near the sideline, putting minimal pressure on the opposing center.

The Wizards have to find a way to make plays like this impact the defense more. They're simply not getting enough out of their secondary actions. Above, for example, Johnson sprinting up from the corner is a good idea in theory. But nobody is screening for Johnson here. What if AD had turned at speed and set a pindown for him, just as the defense expects a screen for Young?

The best offenses pivot into second and third actions. These are built-in counters, depending on how the defense guards the initial one. Consider Sarr in this position, after running a pick and pop:

Bilal Coulibaly's cut through the paint is a scripted thing many teams with shooting bigs do. It's meant to drag away the help defender closest to Sarr — the guy whose job it would be to stunt toward Sarr and contest a three-pointer. But here, Sarr set the screen near half-court and barely made contact. Larry Nance Jr. recovered easily; no rotation needed.

This first action didn't yield much, which is normal. The next step for the Wiz is moving quickly and effectively into something else, and making the right reads from there. This is where the above play ended up:

Sarr dribbles into a hand-off with Johnson, who has sprinted into the space that Coulibaly vacated. This looks promising; George is spaced one pass away, and Johnson has his defender on his back. But Johnson doesn't see the pass to George in time, and Jalen Slawson blows up his dribble for a dunk the other way.

They have the right idea here. They're trying to use Sarr and Johnson in their optimal roles. But defenses see these kinds of actions every game. Without a higher level of precision — physical, well-timed screens, and snappy passing — these plays look ordinary and even aimless.

There are ways to loosen this up. Step one, of course, is to make some shots. (Even Thursday was a mixed bag in this regard, with Johnson shooting 1-of-9 from three.) Getting more consistent offense from wings other than George, who is leveling up before our eyes, would be a godsend. Most of all, the Wizards need Young to find more success probing around and behind bigs, rather than ending up in these situations:

The Wizards have been focused on running these "angle" pick and rolls near the sideline. They are useful for generating pocket passes to the bigs, while spacing guys on the other side. But too often, with Young struggling to separate off the dribble, opposing teams are using aggressive coverages and pinning Young to the sideline.

Tough games are looming against feisty, athletic Western Conference teams in Houston and Memphis. With a 4-9 record, they'll need to find a way to create more advantages in short order.

#2761. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2760. Seahawks elevate two veteran practice squad players ahead of Raiders game

Although the Seattle Seahawks are set to be without several key starters against the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 10, they'll get some much needed depth from two experienced veterans.

The Seahawks elevated cornerback Trevon Diggs and offensive tackle Bobby Hart from the practice squad for Sunday's game against the Raiders, they announced on Saturday. Both players already have suited up for Seattle this season.

The Seahawks signed OG Cordell Volson on Thursday, DT Cole Brevard two days prior and QB Adrian Martinez on Nov. 4, making it plausible the team didn't feel any could make as much of an impact as a player like Diggs.

#2759. Jerry Jones: "I don't think we're far away" from 18 regular-season games

As the NFL embarks on the second half of its current 18-week regular-season schedule, it’s just a matter of time before the current structure changes.

It’s no secret that the NFL wants to expand the regular season from 17 to 18 games. The league is sufficiently confident about it happening that folks like Cowboys owner Jerry Jones speak of it as a given.

“I don’t think we’re far away from it,” Jones said Friday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas, regarding the addition of an extra game. “I don’t know how — what is far away. Next month? No. Next year? Maybe. [The] next year? Maybe. That has to be negotiated with the players.

“But it’s in everybody’s best interests.  You’d cut back on the preseason games. You’d have teams more develop in the first few games as the type of thing you were trying to get done in preseason. But it’s in everybody’s interest, and it certainly is in the players’ best interest in my mind, for sure.  And having said that, I would anticipate that coming.”

His comments presume the NFL Players Association will happily agree to 18 regular-season games. They likely won’t. At a minimum, they’ll seek major concessions in exchange for the willingness to add yet another game that counts.

The unspoken goal had been 2027. The NFL delayed picking a date for Super Bowl LXII in Atlanta in order to accommodate the possibility that the game will slide a week or two deeper into February. That would make 2028 the earliest year for expansion, as a practical matter. (Adding a game for 2027 would be possible only if the dead week between the conference championships is wiped out or if the season starts a week earlier. If an 18th game will result in a second bye, both would be required.)

Expansion by 2027 would require expedited negotiations. Expansion by 2028 would hinge on the NFL and NFLPA striking a deal within the next year or so. The union has shown no inclination, however, to engage in talks aimed at extending the current Collective Bargaining Agreement, which runs through the 2030 season.

Still, if push comes to shove, there will be 18 games. The blueprint was created in 2011. The NFL will lock the players out until the players agree to the things the owners want. Most notably, 18 regular-season games and 16 annual international games.

Beyond that, Jones’s comment about the early games of the season is odd. “You’d have teams more develop in the first few games as the type of thing you were trying to get done in preseason.”

He says that as if it’s a good thing. It definitely is not. Already, teams struggle in September to get up to speed, given that most teams (with the exception of those assigned to the Hall of Fame Game) play only three preseason games. When the preseason reduces to two games, that’s even fewer chances to prepare.

It’s also fewer chances for the non-starters to get the attention of coaches and General Managers in games that don’t count in the standings. It will become harder for undrafted free agents to make the 53-man rosters.

Regardless, the motivation isn’t football. It’s money. More inventory equals more weekends equals more broadcast windows equals more revenue.

And that likely will continue until the preseason shrinks to zero games — and the regular season expands to 20 games.

#2758. 3 Takeaways: Mistakes, Special Teams Continue To Plague Penguins In 4-1 Loss To Senators

After a relatively successful 2-1 Western road trip, the Pittsburgh Penguins were hoping to build off some of the momentum they gained as they went home to face the Ottawa Senators Saturday.

Unfortunately, the inconsistency that has plagued them all season long came roaring back to bite them.

The Senators defeated the Penguins, 4-1, in a game that was - for most of it - much closer than the scoresheet indicated. They held an early 1-0 lead and controlled play for most of the first half, then special teams and mistakes sunk the ship midway through the second. They were never really able to recover from that, and as a result, were outshot, 34-17, when all was said and done.

"I think consistency has been an issue. I mean, I think tonight's another example of that," head coach Dan Muse said. "I thought there were stretches of the game where that was there. If you go through the game, I thought the first period... I walked out of that first pretty happy with things. Not just the goal at the end of the period, but the period as a whole. I think that's kind of the way you need to play against a team like this.

"And then, I thought the beginning of the second, it was there, and I thought we got away from it in the back half of the second. I think we got stubborn with it. Some of the things that were working in the first period, we didn't stay with it long enough."

As indicated by their head coach, the Penguins got off to a pretty solid start in the first period. Even if the teams were trading some chances, Pittsburgh had the majority of possession and better of the play throughout the opening frame. They had a Tommy Novak goal called off for offside midway through.

But he made up for it before the horn sounded to end the first. In the final seconds, Ben Kindel sprung Egor Chinakhov and Novak on a two-on-one. Chinakhov served a perfect pass on a silver platter to Novak on the left side, and he redirected it in for his team-leading eighth goal of the season to put the Penguins up 1-0 with 6.3 seconds on the clock.

Pittsbugh started off the second period strong, too, outshooting Ottawa 5-0 for the first eight and a half minutes of it and controlling play. But, shortly after Ottawa killed off a slashing penalty by Claude Giroux, Connor Dewar made an ill-advised pass in the defensive zone that was picked off by Senators' forward Michael Amado, and he buried it for his seventh of the season to tie the game at 1-1.

From there, Ottawa seized much of the momentum in the middle frame. With a little under four minutes to go in the period, Claude Giroux took advantage of another errant Penguins' pass - this time, by Ben Kindel in the neutral zone - and carried it all the way in to beat Murashov and give the Senators the 2-1 lead.

And, in the third period, the Senators really shut it down. Tim Stutzle earned a weird goal from a bad angle on one knee late in the third, then Thomas Chabot put the game away with the empty-netter at the end. The Penguins mustered just six shots on goal in the final 34 minutes and 57 seconds of regulation, which just isn't going to get the job done most nights.

"I think we felt pretty good about the way we played for a good chunk of that road trip," Sidney Crosby said. "But, this was a different team that we played in comparison to those three games on that trip. It was a little bit more wide-open. I think this was a tighter game, a little more physical, and we have to be able to produce chances in that type of game.

"They just played better, you know? That's basically what it comes down to."

- I know we're beating the already long-dead horse here, but the power play is a legitimate problem.

Maybe it's personnel. Maybe it's coaching. Maybe it's mental. Maybe it's 'get a few, and they'll start going in.' Maybe the guys running it just aren't processing the game fast enough anymore.

Whatever it is, they need to figure it out fast if they're going to have any kind of shot at digging themselves out of the hole they're in. The Penguins had two power plays in this game before Senators had one, and they weren't able to build on the 1-0 lead they established early on back up by some really solid five-on-five play. They also had a power play directly following the Senators' man advantage that the Penguins killed off.

Then, as it often does, one bad mistake burned them shortly after the Sens killed the third penalty. The Penguins were not able to handle those momentum swings brought on by special teams, and the mistakes came back to burn them again.

Penguins' Prospect Headed To Spengler CupOne of Pittsburgh's defensive prospects is heading off to NCAA Hockey's most prestigious international tournament.

- To follow up on those mistakes, the Penguins were their own worst enemy in this one. They were controlling the game for the entirety of its first half.

In reference to that post-power play mistake, Dewar had the puck along the left wall and, for some reason, threw the puck right into the middle of the ice in the defensive zone in an attempt to spring Erik Karlsson on the breakout. There's no reason to make that pass there as opposed to simply getting it ahead and out of the zone.

Ottawa's second goal was a huge mistake, too. The Penguins' second line was attempting to enter the offensive zone, and the puck carrier was Kindel. Instead of simply just getting the puck deep, he elected to put a backhand pass under pressure in the direction of Egor Chinakhov down the middle.

It hit the skate of Ridly Greig and went right to Giroux's stick, and he didn't miss, either.

All season long, the Penguins have actually been a relatively solid five-on-five team. But they make way too many glaring mistakes like this that end up in the back of their net. Going into this one, the Penguins were right in the middle of the league (15th) in giveaways with 276 and - actually - owned the second-least number of defensive zone giveaways (107) in the NHL, but it sure doesn't feel like it.

And that's probably because half the giveaways happen at the worst times and turn into the most high-danger of high-danger chances. They need to be better than that for their goaltenders, especially with two young netminders.

Penguins' Defenseman Trevor van Riemsdyk Returns To Team PracticeOne of Pittsburgh's veteran blueliners appears close to a return to action.

But, according to the captain, mistakes are part of the game and always have been. And the team just needs to figure out a way to have a better response.

"Yeah, I mean, that's the game, though. It's been like that for a long time, and it's not going to change," Crosby said. "It's just one of those things where, some nights, you pay for them. Other nights, you find ways to make up for it or score a little bit more. So, that's the game. and we have to find a way to be better. And that's really what it comes down to."

One major difference between this team and the one from 2024-25, Mike Sullivan's final season as head coach, is that, as frustrating as the losses were, they were finding and inventing different ways to lose every time.

This season? It's the same thing nearly every night: Mistakes suck the life out of them, and they cannot recover or take back momentum enough to deliver a positive result. If it's fixable - which, honestly, it kind of feels like it is - they need to fix it fast. Because they're falling fast.

- Aside from the Stutzle goal, Murashov was good in net again. Of course, he would want the Stutzle goal back. But, it was a bit of an awkward play in general, as Murashov was still getting reset and Stutzle just threw it back at the net, and he still put together a 30-save effort.

Regardless of that goal, just as he was in his wins over the Los Angeles Kings and San Jose Sharks on the Penguins' preceding California road trip, he was oozing confidence and challenging shooters. He made several huge saves, including one with his right pad on Tim Stutzle late in the second period. And he made them look easy with his quickness and athleticism.

Those were two words that Penguins' Hall of Fame-elect Marc-Andre Fleury used to describe Murashov prior to the game. Fleury was the Penguins' franchise goaltender for over a decade. Murashov has a chance to be the franchise goaltender of the future.

If these past three games are any indication of his ceiling and his ability, he's going to have an NHL career. He's playing pretty well at the moment, and he only figures to continue getting better as he progresses in his development.

The Penguins don't play again until Thursday, when they host the St. Louis Blues. I semi-expect Arturs Silovs to get the net for that one only because he won't have played for more than a week and a half at that point.

But, don't be surprised if Murashov gets the nod, either. The Penguins play a back-to-back over the weekend on the road against the Nashville Predators and Dallas Stars, and if they're riding the hot hand, they might want Murashov to get two of those three games.

Penguins Young Goalie Is Showing Big Signs Of Breaking OutThis is promising to see.

BONUS TAKEAWAY: The Penguins don't play again until Thursday.

It wouldn't come as much of a surprise if something happens between now and then. It's not exactly a secret that this team is struggling to find any manner of consistency, and they're running out of time to figure things out. They're 7-11-2, two points out of the East's basement, and 10 points out of the final wild card spot.

There may not be an early move that's seismic, so to speak. But think Lars Eller getting traded in November during the 2024-25 season: Maybe it's a bottom-six guy to free up some valuable roster space for a younger player, to shake up the room a bit, and to get some early value while teams are looking to plug some holes well in advance of the trade deadline.

Of course, the Erik Karlssons, Rickard Rakells, and Bryan Rusts are the big talking points. But don't rule out the Blake Lizottes, Sam Girards, Connor Dewars, or even the Tommy Novaks, either.

#2757. Ground stop results in side judge Don Willard serving as referee for two games on Sunday

Friday’s nationwide ground stop won’t keep NFL teams from getting to their road games on Sunday. It will, however, impact the ability of officials to get to where they need to be.

The NFL has announced that officiating assignments have changed for Week 10. And the situation will result in a backup referee serving as the referee in two games on the same day.

“Due to the ongoing nationwide impact to air travel this weekend, the NFL has adjusted its officiating assignments for Week 10 games, reassigning officials to games within driving distance of their hometowns,” the NFL said in a statement. “The changes will necessitate that three backup referees — umpires Barry Anderson and Duane Heydt and side judge Don Willard [pictured] — will work as referees in the following games: Carolina-New Orleans – Duane Heydt; Jacksonville-Tennessee – Barry Anderson; Miami-Indianapolis and Pittsburgh-Cincinnati – Don Willard.

“Each of the league’s 17 officiating crews have a backup referee identified, and that individual trains throughout the year to work at the referee position should the need arise.”

The situation creates the likely unprecedented situation of a referee working two games in one day. Willard will handle Dolphins-Colts at 1:00 p.m. ET, and then he’ll make the 109-mile trip from Indianapolis to Cincinnati for the Sunday night game.

Making the unprecedented even more unusual is the fact that Willard’s usual crew (led by referee Scott Novak) wasn’t scheduled to work at all this weekend.

The announcement doesn’t address where the referees for those three games will be working, or what their roles will be. Shawn Smith was scheduled to be the referee for Panthers-Saints, Alex Moore was set to be the referee for Jaguars-Titans, Carl Cheffers was due to be the referee for Dolphins-Colts, and Clete Blakeman was slated to be the referee for Steelers-Bengals.

The league’s statement also doesn’t specify other shifts that were required as to the established crews that work together throughout the regular season.

The NFL divides the money it collects from player discipline and splits it equally between the NFLPA's efforts to support and assist retired players, and the NFL Foundation and other nonprofits that support youth sports, player health and safety at all levels of sports, and community health initiatives.

#2754. Report: Vikings first reached out to Raiders about Kirk Cousins on "midday Monday"

As it turns out, the Vikings contacted the Raiders about a possible trade for quarterback Kirk Cousins before Monday night’s meltdown from quarterback Carson Wentz.

Via ESPNFL, the Vikings initially contacted the Raiders during “midday Monday,” prior to Minnesota’s Week 9 game against the Bills. The Vikings told the Raiders they wanted to see how things went during the Monday night game before having any further conversations.

Then came Wentz’s 8.9-passer rating performance in a 23-6 loss, and Minnesota mobilized. The Vikings, per the report, contacted the Raiders before 6:00 a.m. PT on Tuesday and commenced the talks that culminated in a deal being done.

Said Raiders G.M. John Spytek during a Tuesday press conference: “I never made one call on Kirk Cousins. And I got a few phone calls. But one real one this morning.”

The Vikings initially offered a fifth-round pick for Cousins, per the report. The report doesn’t specify the Raiders’ opening position.

Once the Vikings moved to a third-round pick, the Raiders pounced.

Beyond avoiding the $10 million guaranteed bonus and clearing the path for rookie No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza (which are mentioned in the article), the Raiders ultimately bought a third-round pick for $650,000 (which is not).

That’s the most attractive aspect of the entire transaction, in our view. Nearly 10 years ago, the Browns bought a second-round pick from the Texans by assuming quarterback Brock Osweiler’s $16 million full guarantee for the 2017 season. Any team would sprint for the chance to purchase a third-round pick in the 2027 draft for only $650,000.

In this case, that bargain came with nine starts from Cousins, four wins, and months of excellent mentorship for Mendoza.

As to the lingering sense in some circles that the Raiders could have gotten even more for Cousins, they risked driving a bargain so hard that the Vikings would have walked away and made a trade with another team.

So it was a win for the Vikings, who got their first choice. It was a win for the Raiders. And it definitely was a win for Cousins, who went from waiting to be benched for Mendoza to having nine games as the starter for a contender — plus the strong possibility that the Vikings will make the playoffs.

#2753. Notre Dame Women’s Basketball: Irish roll in 108-84 win over DePaul

Hannah Hidalgo and her friends at Notre Dame are averaging over 100 points per game the season, and that held true against DePaul on Saturday in the Shamrock Classic, 108-84.

SOUTH BEND, Ind. – Notre Dame (4-0) continued its winning ways on Saturday, as the 13th-ranked Irish downed DePaul 108-84 in the 2026 SoFi Shamrock Classic. Hannah Hidalgo paced the game with 31 points, seven rebounds and four steals. Her swipes give her 500 in her career, and she is now the only college basketball player — men's or women's — in history to have 2500 points, 500 rebounds, 500 assists and 500 steals.

Anaya Hardy also notched a line in the record books, as she had a career-high 16 rebounds, including a program-record 12 offensive boards. Hardy (13), Leah Macy (24), Jacy Abii (18) and Madison St. Rose (16) also scored in double-figures.

As a team, Notre Dame scored 100 points for the third consecutive game, which has not been done in the history of the storied program.

The Irish offense started slow by recent standards; Hidalgo had a pair of driving layups as Notre Dame's first two baskets from the floor on the day. DePaul then went on a 6-0 run to take a 9-5 lead into the first media break.

Hidalgo had seven of Notre Dame's first eight points. The Irish used their size to take over in the paint, as 20 of the team's 24 first quarter points came inside. Hidalgo finished the frame with nine points, and Abii followed with seven points, four rebounds and a pair of blocks.The Irish held a 24-17 lead after 10 minutes.

DePaul went on a 7-0 run to start the second quarter, while Notre Dame couldn't find the basket, going through a 1-10 drought. The Blue Demons had four different players hit a bucket in that period, and it was 33-29 at the media break.

A Hardy floater ended the drought, and DePaul was on a drought of its own with one basket in its next seven tries. Notre Dame, meanwhile, started to heat up from deep, as Hidalgo and Macy hit back-to-back triples. Macy's basket was the first three-pointer of her Notre Dame career. Overall, Notre Dame went on a 13-2 run from 7:03 to 2:59 as the half wound down.

At the end of the half, Notre Dame held a 49-34 lead. The Irish dominated on the boards, out rebounding DePaul 32-21, and scoring 13 second chance points.

Individually, Hidalgo led all scorers with 19 points. Abii had seven points and seven rebounds, and Hardy led all players with nine boards, six of them offensive.

Hidalgo opened the second-half scoring with a three countered by a DePaul three. The Blue Demons then failed to score for 2:43, during which the Irish started to work in transition. Macy had a pair of fast break conversions with a Hardy put-back sandwiched between. Notre Dame widened the lead to its largest of the day, 60-41, but the Blue Demons wouldn't go away. Back-to-back made triples from DePaul with an added transition basket over the course of 48 seconds forced a Notre Dame timeout at 60-49 with 4:27 to play in the quarter.

Macy broke the 8-0 run with a pair of made three throws, and DePaul continued to score, making seven consecutive shots. Hidalgo had the last laugh in the third, driving into the lane and making it 74-61 with 10 minutes left.

Reigning ACC Freshman of the Week Abii opened the scoring in the fourth quarter. A driving layup and a corner three from St. Rose followed, opening up a 20-point lead for Notre Dame, their largest of the day.

St. Rose continued the excellent final quarter, finishing with 13 points in the frame, as Notre Dame continued to pull away for the win.

The Irish return home on Wednesday to host Southern. The game tips off on ACCNX at 7 p.m.

#2750. Kings head coach Doug Christie gets brutally honest about job security

SACRAMENTO ― The Sacramento Kings have dropped another game and if you think head coach Doug Christie is worried about being in some kind of hot seat, he's not. And he shouldn't be.

It's a familiar position for Christie, who's been dealt a bad hand since his head coaching tenure began. He inherited a then-Mike Brown team that was a season removed from the postseason before eventually trading its franchise player, De'Aaron Fox. They finished 40-42, Christie went 27-24 as interim, having taken over after a 13-18 start.

Last season, as an official first-year coach, without the interim tag, multiple players in his projected lineup, including Domantas Sabonis and Keegan Murray, missed large portions of the season, and the Kings finished with its worst record in franchise history since moving to Sacramento at 22-60.

And now, the Kings are having one of the worst starts in franchise history, dropping to 1-11 after their Friday night loss to the Portland Trail Blazers, 120-107, on Nov. 13 during the NBA Cup. It's the worst start since the 1990-91 season, in which that team started 1-13.

"I think this seat is hot always, so it doesn't really matter," Christie told USA TODAY about potentially being in the hot seat. "Obviously, we want to win games. Nobody wants to win more than me, from the standpoint that the record doesn't go on the player's numbers. The record goes on coach's number."

When Scott Perry became Kings general manager in April 2025, one of his first moves was to sign Christie to a three-year deal, worth about $2 million per year with a team option in the final year, 2027-28. Christie remained leading the charge after coaching to the worst franchise record in team history since 2008-2009 (17-65), as Perry attributed that tumultuous season to injuries, according to The Athletic.

It's much of the same this season, with a season-ending injury to Ben Simmons and second-year center Maxime Raynaud missing the start of the season with a knee injury.

"We come in, continue to teach, continue to push," Christie said. "As we get all these guys back and get them healthy, and then we continue down the path of trying to put together what we thought we would be putting together when we started this process."

The Kings are reportedly hesitant to part ways with Christie, according to The Athletic's Sam Amick. Former Sacramento Kings legend and current Sacramento State head coach Mike Bibby sat front row to get a witness of the the beatdown handed to the Kings.

The former guard, who played in Sacramento from 2001-2008, showed support for his former teammate, saying he wasn't the one to blame during a postgame appearance with Morgan Ragan and Deuce Mason on NBC Sports California.

"I don't blame Doug (Christie)," Bibby said. "I don't think Doug is the problem. Doug's been there for a long time, I think Doug could help, but getting rid of Doug's not the problem."

However, Bibby did say it was "time for some changes". Although he wasn't sure where those changes needed to come from, he advised the team to trade guys like Domantas Sabonis, Zach LaVine and Malik Monk to put them in better positions while the Kings start over. It happened to Bibby in his day when the Kings were no longer winning and they traded him to the Atlanta Hawks in 2008.

"When I was here I didn't wanna leave, but it was time to go," Bibby said. "For those guys put them in good situations like Sabonis, LaVine, put them in situations that could help them and get some good stuff back. It's going to take a couple of years to get the Kings going again."

Kings: Darius Acuff Jr. is making history, but is losing taking a toll?

If there's one thing Christie knows, it's how hard the Sacramento fans go for the Kings. He's experienced it as a player, and as both assistant and head coach he's seen how they've stuck beside the team through multiple years of losing seasons and the breakthrough when they finally cracked the postseason after a 16-year drought.

Christie's message to the fans: "it won't always be like this."

"This is a process that we're going through to try to get to where we want to go, and their loyalty means everything," Christie told USA TODAY. " When I see them around town, they're always (saying) 'coach keep going, keep pushing,' and that's what I do every day. I'll always be the first one in the building, working until we figure this thing out."

Kings forward Keegan Murray had a similar message to the fans to keep supporting, despite the shortcomings.

"I love our fans. They've been great to us... to me. I appreciate them coming out to support, we know that Rome's not built in a day but at the end of the day we're trying," Murray told USA TODAY. "With their support, it'll only get better."

Murray, Sabonis and Monk are the few Kings players that have been around for their lone playoff appearance in the last 15 years. Murray often tells the team, especially Acuff who was down in the dumps after a recent home loss, about how loud Golden 1 Center can get when their team is rolling.

"When we're really good, this place is better than any arena in the NBA," Murray said. "I feel like that's a big motivating factor in what we're trying to get to. ... I'm just hoping we can get back on track."

#2749. Kentucky’s Playoff Hopes On Life Support

A week ago, Will Stein's Wildcats saw their six-game winning streak end in an ugly second half down in Knoxville. A week later, they returned home to take on a Florida club needing a win to keep their college football playoff hopes alive. For the Gators, it was a return home for two former Cats, including new head coach Jon Sumrall. While Kentucky started strong, another bad second half did them in and likely ended any chance of making the playoff. Let's break it down as Kentucky's playoff hopes are on life support after a 21-14 loss to Florida.

The Wildcats' defense stopped Florida on their first possession. Kentucky got the ball and went 86 yards in 15 plays, taking up over eight minutes. The last five came on a nice five-yard pass from Kenny Minchey to CJ Baxter, and it was 7-0 Kentucky.

From there, it was a battle of punts as neither team could get anything going. The Wildcats had some chances but couldn't take advantage, and that would prove costly.

Photo Credit: Jordan Prather-Imagn Images

Late in the first half, the Wildcat defense held once again. However, on the Gators' punt, there were offsetting penalties, including running into the kicker on Kentucky. Instead of the Cats getting the ball at the 20, on the second punt Florida downed it at the UK 4.

That would prove big, as Kentucky's potential All-American lineman Lance Heard was called for holding in the end zone, resulting in a safety, negating a big play by the Cats. The only problem was the foul took place on the three-yard line, but the call stood. We had a baseball score at the half, 7-2.

Kentucky got the ball to start the second half, but Minchey was sacked and fumbled. Florida recovered and had great field position at the UK 30. Seven plays later, Jadan Baugh, who always plays well against Kentucky, took it in from a yard out, and the Gators led in a game for the first time since October. Aaron Philo got a two-point conversion, and it was 10-7.

Kentucky took advantage of what seemed like an ill-conceived onside kick, getting the ball at the 45. Minchey took it in from the one, and UK was up 14-10, and the BBN was starting to feel better. After all, Kentucky had dominated second halves all year. However, on this night, they were the ones who were dominated.

A Florida field goal cut the lead to one, but the Kentucky offense couldn't figure out former defensive coordinator Brad White's schemes. Much like last week, you have to give Florida credit: their defensive front dominated the Kentucky offensive line, which was just named a semifinalist for the Joe Moore Award. It's a big reason why Kentucky's playoff hopes are on life support.

In the last five games, Philo has rushed for a grand total of 49 yards. Throughout the second half, he ran over, around, and through the Wildcat defense.

Going 14 plays in 67 yards, Philo took it the last two to give Florida a five-point lead. Sumrall again went for two and was successful, and the lead was 21-14. For the game, Philo rushed for a team-high 102 yards, and the Gators had 211 overall. It's the second straight week the UK defense has given up more than 200 on the ground.

Even with the struggles, Kentucky had their chances. After getting the ball inside the Florida 30, UK faced a third-and-11. A run by Baxter, trying to catch the Gators off balance, gained only two. On fourth down, White dialed up a blitz, and like most of the game, it was successful; Minchey was incomplete the Cats turned it over on downs.

Florida kept the ball for nearly four minutes before the defense got the stop it needed. However, four straight incompletions ended any chance of a comeback. As a result, Kentucky's playoff hopes are on life support as the Cats lose to Florida 21-14.

With the loss, Kentucky drops to 7-3 on the season and 5-3 in the SEC. They'll travel to Missouri next Saturday night for a 7:30 pm game. The Tigers ran into the Georgia buzzsaw today, losing 48-21. As we've mentioned, Kentucky's playoff hopes are pretty much done. They could win out and still have a chance, but it'll be tough.

On the other side of the ball, it was a happy homecoming for former UK player and assistant coach Jon Sumrall. It was also a good night for former defensive coordinator Brad White. The Gators move to 6-4 on the year and 4-4 in league play. They host Vanderbilt next week.

For the second straight week, the Kentucky football team was physically dominated by their opponent. The Cats only mustered 61 yards rushing on the night. In addition, after giving up 86 yards on the first drive, the Gators only allowed 156 the rest of the way.

With 221 total yards, the Cats' defense made Philo look like Tim Tebow. With everything to play for, it was an utterly disappointing performance by the Wildcats. Too many missed opportunities, along with penalties and turnovers, cost them.

The Cats are in line for a major bowl, most likely not the playoff. However, they must right the ship and get back to the play they showed during their six-game winning streak.

In the end, on a "Black Out" night at Kroger Field, Kentucky's playoff hopes are on life support after a 21-14 loss to Florida.
