#2748. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2744. Common theme in Kentucky's losses rears its ugly head against Florida

LEXINGTON -- Kentucky has lost three games this season. Each time, the opponent won the turnover battle.

In UK's 21-14 loss to Florida on Saturday, there was only one turnover. Kentucky committed it. Though it didn't happen on the last play of the game, Kenny Minchey's lost fumble shifted the momentum in favor of the Gators.

"The sack fumble, obviously not a good play for us tonight," Minchey said afterward. "You know, you want to be able to feel that. (You) want to be able obviously block up front, and yeah, just unfortunate. I have to be able to hold on to the football."

In the first half, Florida's defense was on the field when it found its first points. Kentucky was called for a holding in its end zone, which by rule, results in a safety.

Kentucky began the second half with the ball and a 7-2 lead. On the second play of the third quarter, Minchey was hit by Jayden Woods, who forced the strip sack that Florida was able to recover on the Wildcats' 30-yard line.

"I think a lot of our turnovers have become because our edge players are hitting the quarterback as they're throwing or disrupting the passing rhythm of the quarterback," UK coach Will Stein said. "I think we just aren't doing a good enough job."

The Gators capitalized when Jaden Baugh scored to give his team its first lead of the night. Following that moment, Florida's offense became more fluid.

Kentucky punched back, taking a 14-10 lead. But on their next offensive possession, the Gators crossed midfield for the first time all night, finishing that drive with a field goal.

They were able to stop Kentucky and secure the final touchdown of the night with 9:11 left in the contest. The Wildcats had their chances, but couldn't put up points.

"We've got to get in the red zone, and we've got to really make plays in the red zone," UK tight end Willie Rodriguez said. "They schemed us up pretty well, but we also made plays, too. Like I said, we just got to go back to finishing drives."

And when Florida stumped Kentucky on 4th down with 5:29 left in the game, the Gators maintained a drive that lasted nearly four minutes. Their ability to get it done on the ground forced Stein to use all of his timeouts, which left Minchey and the offense 1:48 to get 64 yards.

Florida didn't even let them pick up one. Minchey threw four consecutive incompletions.

On a night when yards were tough to find and points even more so, UK's lone fumble felt like the play of the game.

The Gators' offense woke up and their defense buckled down. Though the Cats lost the turnover battle by one, it was enough to change the game and prove that it's one of the main reasons they've lost their games this season.

#2743. Sixers finding success manufacturing their own energy

It was only the first quarter of the 13th game of the Sixers' season, so there seemed to be no cause for alarm (and never mind the booing). Still, they were down 17 to a Toronto team on the second half of a back-to-back and playing without its two best players. There was at least the possibility Thursday that it was one of those nights every NBA team has on occasion, where the mood and the energy and the desire are just … off.

It would be easy to reach that conclusion, after Boston smacked the Sixers around Tuesday, in what was supposed to be the Jaylen Brown Revenge Game. Also, LeBron James sat out against the Raptors. The official reason was "low back/sciatica management," though this seems comparable to that time years ago when the Spurs rested Tim Duncan and listed him this way in the boxscore: "DNP-OLD."

When Nick Nurse called timeout with 2:40 left in the first and his team down 32-16, he said he was thinking in the simplest terms.

"I just want the players to play well," he said, adding that everyone seemed to be searching for a rhythm, or seeking to "shake something off from the last game or whatever," as he put it.

They fell 17 back moments later, but soon found their inspiration, soon manufactured their own energy. Reserves Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker found it by looking back to their time on some wretched Portland teams. VJ Edgecombe found it by looking forward to a potential spot in the NBA slam-dunk contest.

And Tyrese Maxey found it by looking over to the sideline, to his infant daughter.

The end result was a 123-112 Sixers victory over the Scottie Barnes– and Kawhi Leonard-less Raptors. Maxey scored 27, and Joel Embiid, who limped off in the first quarter after bumping knees with a Raptor, returned and finished with 20. Edgecombe enjoyed a Swiss Army Knife kinda night – 15 points, eight rebounds, eight assists, three steals and a block – and the bench brigade of Simons, Walker and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope contributed 37 points, including 9-for-12 three-point sniping.

"You learn once you're coming off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there," Simons said after going 5-for-6 from the arc and scoring 17.

What he read before checking in at the aforementioned timeout was straight out of the Stephen King collection. So the idea, Simons said, was to "bring some energy and some life to the team."

He provided the night's first thunderbolt, nailing a three-ball at the first-period buzzer to cut the deficit to nine.

"Those are big momentum plays," Nurse said, "that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment."

From that point forward, the Sixers, now 10-3, seemed inevitable. Edgecombe turned a second-quarter steal into a breakaway slam. Maxey threw an alley-oop to Brown from midcourt for a bucket late in the third, when Philadelphia went ahead for good. And with the Raptors hanging around late in the fourth, Simons and Caldwell-Pope (11 points) connected from three to put it away.

Re Simons: Now in his ninth NBA season, he is playing for his fourth team. He has been productive everywhere he's been, but this year his minutes (21.7) and points (10.2) are down from their usual levels. He says he doesn't care – not after playing on losing teams five of the seven seasons he spent in Portland, his first stop. The Blazers were 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46 the last three of those seasons, when Walker was a teammate. (Another Sixer, Rayan Rupert, was on two of those teams.)

"You learn a lot in those situations about yourself, the people around you, your teammates," Simons said, adding that "you feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning. And so that's something that you can't take for granted for sure, because it's hard to win in the NBA."

Sometimes it's hard to even get on the court, as Walker has learned. He is averaging 15 minutes a game over five seasons, but now looms as the best option to back up Embiid at center, despite standing 6-7. Not to worry, he said after contributing nine points and eight boards in just under 16 minutes Thursday; his dad, Samaki, had been a small-ball center himself while playing a decade in the Association. The younger Walker knows the assignment, knows what the job entails.

He's also healthy this season, having undergone offseason knee surgery. And while it wasn't clear where he might fit in the pecking order after the Sixers revamped their roster over the summer, he had high hopes.

"I don't know if I was delusional," he said, "but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part. I read some things, and they say it's a surprise. But if you were around me this summer and saw the mindset I had, then it wouldn't be a surprise. So this is expected, and I just want to continue to get better."

There were also questions about Edgecombe's role coming into the season. But his attitude is always exemplary, his approach relentless. Informed after Thursday's game that the only guard in the league with more dunks than him was Houston's Amen Thompson, he scoffed.

"Man, he don't even count," Edgecombe said.

He might have a point. Thompson stands 6-7. Edgecombe is listed at 6-4, but attacks the rim so regularly that he is musing about the dunk contest on All-Star Weekend, February in Phoenix.

"Obviously I don't want to sit here and give a yes, and I don't want to give a no," he said. "But that's something I'm thinking about, for sure."

Maxey couldn't help but think about his daughter Marvel. Born May 14 to Tyrese and his girlfriend Myra Gordon, she attended her first game with her mom Thursday – "a really cool moment," as Maxey said.

She might not be back for a while, though.

"It's too late," he said. "She was yawning and doing a whole bunch of stuff."

So too were the Sixers for a while. They awakened from their slumber. They found their footing, manufactured their own energy. On many, many nights across the long season, that's how it has to be.

#2742. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

#2741. Miami 36, Duke 25: Five Key Plays

Duke fell to 7-3 (4-3) on the season with a 36-25 loss to the Miami Hurricanes. Nate Sheppard rushed 16 times for 131 yards and two touchdowns, and caught 12 passes for 93 yards in a tremendous performance. Walker Eget completed 26 of 42 pass attempts for 195 yards, one touchdown and one costly interception.

The Blue Devils defense played the 'Canes tough before wearing down in the 4th quarter. The halftime score was Miami 13, Duke 10 and it was Miami 22, Duke 17 at the end of the 3rd quarter. Miami won time of possession 34:13 to 25:47 and outgained Duke 532 to 341 in total yards.

Miami quarterback Darian Mensah completed 30 of 41 pass attempts for 382 yards and one touchdown. Wide receiver Cooper Barkate was the 'Canes leading receiver with eight receptions for 134 yards. Javian Mallory rushed 10 times for 71 yards and two touchdowns, and grabbed three receptions for 79 yards and a touchdown.

Play One: Trailing 29-17, with 6 minutes and 54 seconds remaining in the game, Duke faced a 2nd down and nine yards to go at their own 46-yard line. Eget threw a pass down the right sideline toward Brody Keefe, but the pass was intercepted by Miami defensive back Xavier Lucas. Five plays later, Javian Mallory dashed 39 yards for a touchdown to expand Miami's lead to 36-17.

Play Two: With two minutes and 43 seconds remaining in the 3rd quarter, with the score 16-10 Miami, the 'Canes had the ball on their own 37 yard line. Mensah completed a screen pass to Javian Mallory who rambled 63 yards for a touchdown to expand the lead to 22-10. The 2-point conversion attempt failed.

Play Three: With Miami leading 10-3, on 1st down and 10, Sheppard exploded on an inside run for 47 yards and a touchdown, to tie the game at 10 points apiece.

Play Four: On 2nd down and goal to go, with 41 seconds remaining in the 3rd quarter, Sheppard ran five yards for a touchdown to cut Miami's lead to 22-17. Duke moved into scoring position two plays earlier when Duke executed a double pass from Eget to Sheppard to Javen Nicholas for 13 yards to the Miami 5-yard line. Sheppard rushed for 47 yards on the first play of the drive.

Play Five: Duke's stout defense kept the Blue Devils in the game. Three times Miami drove into the red zone, but settled for field goals instead of touchdowns, due to Duke getting stops on 3rd down. Two of the three times the stop came on 3rd down and goal to go.

#2740. Packers, Broncos explored possible Tony Pollard trade

One week before the trade deadline, teams had interest in Titans running back Tony Pollard. But Tennessee was not yet talking.

The Titans eventually engaged, but no one met their price.

Via ESPNFL, the Packers and Broncos “checked in” on Pollard. The Titans wouldn’t move Pollard for less than a third-round pick.

Both teams had been linked to Colts running back Jonathan Taylor. The Colts, after creating the impression that Taylor would be traded, opted to take the best offer they could get.

The fact that Green Bay and Denver explored acquiring two different tailbacks isn’t much of a vote of confidence in their current depth charts. As to the Packers, it underscores the potentially tenuous status of Josh Jacobs.

Pollard, a fourth-round pick of the Cowboys in 2019, started his career as the backup/understudy to Ezekiel Elliott. Pollard had a breakthrough season in 2022, rushing for 1,007 yards and making it to the Pro Bowl despite Elliott still being the starter. (Elliott gained 876 yards that season.)

Pollard became the full-time starter in 2023, a franchise-tag season. He signed with the Titans in 2024.

He has four straight 1,000-yard seasons. Through eight games in 2026, he has 595 yards. Which puts him on pace for what would be a career-high 1,190 yards.

Pollard is in the final year of a three-year, $21.75 million contract. He’s due to be a free agent in March.

#2737. Don Willard to serve as the head referee for 2 NFL games on same day after league switches up assignments

NFL referee Don Willard is set to serve as the head referee for two NFL games in the same day. It is not readily known whether this has happened before, according to The Athletic.

He's being pressed into double duty because of the league scrambling to reassign officiating crews due to travel issues caused by Friday's unprecedented four-hour nationwide ground stop for domestic flights in the United States.

This impacted travel plans across sports leagues, including a college football game between Ole Miss and Oklahoma, which was moved to Sunday.

It didn't impact start times for any NFL games, but it did force the league to switch up some referee assignments.

Willard and his crew — umpire Terry Killens, field judge Jabir Walker and side judge Justin Larrew — will begin the day calling the Miami Dolphins-Indianapolis Colts game, set to kick off at 1 p.m. ET in Indiana.

After the game, Willard and Co. will then drive 110 miles to Cincinnati, Ohio, to call the Pittsburgh Steelers-Cincinnati Bengals game for Week 10's "Sunday Night Football," which begins at 8:20 p.m. ET.

While only three officiating crew changes were needed, one could be for the history books.

Willard has been an NFL official for nine years, including officiating six playoff games. He typically serves as a side judge for Scott Novak's crew.

The NFL made the reassignments based on driving distance from officials' hometowns. The other two moves were to have umpire Barry Anderson take over for Alex Moore in the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Tennessee Titans, while Duane Heydt steps in for Shawn Smith in the Carolina Panthers-New Orleans Saints NFC South battle.

Originally, Carl Cheffers was supposed to referee the Miami-Indianapolis game, while Clete Blakeman was supposed to lead the Pittsburgh-Cincinnati game.

Willard will now be the head referee for both games.

#2733. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2732. Steelers' soft zone scheme could have big problems with Bengals QB Joe Burrow

The Pittsburgh Steelers will travel to face the Cincinnati Bengals in an NFL Week 10 rematch that has major implications for the AFC North race.

The former prevailed by a 30-27 margin when these teams first faced off in September in a back-and-forth affair that ended with the Pittsburgh defense stopping a late bid by quarterback Joe Burrow and the Bengals offense to tie the game or take the lead late.

The winner will take a one-game lead in the division. If the Steelers win, they'll own the head-to-head tiebreaker at the end of the season. If the Bengals win, they'll enjoy a favorable schedule to stay one step ahead of first-year coach Mike McCarthy's team.

Here's USA TODAY's guide on what to look for in the matchup, which will air nationally on NBC's "Sunday Night Football."

Required reading: 3 questions that will make or break the second half of the Steelers season

The Bengals star came as close as anyone has all season to solving Pittsburgh defensive coordinator Patrick Graham's revamped system designed to avoid getting beat on long pass plays.

Burrow completed 28 of 37 passes for 282 yards and three touchdowns during the initial Week 3 matchup. He found four different receivers for gains of at least 20 yards, and two of his three scoring tosses came from outside the red zone.

The Steelers have done a nice job of keeping the play in front of them since, a major reason they're allowing just 14.25 points per game during their current four-game winning streak.

Burrow has the receiving talent to challenge that success once again. Ja'Marr Chase has 647 yards and seven touchdowns already in 2026. Counterpart Tee Higgins has been even better with 758 yards and six scores.

It should be quite the battle of wits, with Burrow likely holding the advantage as he gets the start at home at Paycor Stadium.

Ricky Pearsall, SF (knee) - Out for seasonRicky Pearsall of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026, in Santa Clara, California.

Chris Brazzell, CAR (knee) - Out for seasonChris Brazzell II of the Carolina Panthers warms up during the Carolina Panthers Training Camp at Carolina Panthers Practice Fields on July 23, 2026, in Charlotte, North Carolina.

Jayden Higgins, HOU (knee) - Out for seasonJayden Higgins of the Houston Texans catches a pass for a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Indianapolis Colts at NRG Stadium on January 04, 2026, in Houston, Texas.

Ricky Pearsall, SF (knee) - Out for seasonRicky Pearsall of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026, in Santa Clara, California.

Chris Brazzell, CAR (knee) - Out for seasonChris Brazzell II of the Carolina Panthers warms up during the Carolina Panthers Training Camp at Carolina Panthers Practice Fields on July 23, 2026, in Charlotte, North Carolina.

Jayden Higgins, HOU (knee) - Out for seasonJayden Higgins of the Houston Texans catches a pass for a touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Indianapolis Colts at NRG Stadium on January 04, 2026, in Houston, Texas.

As good as Burrow was against Pittsburgh in that first meeting, the Steelers quarterback was even more efficient. He averaged 8.6 yards per attempt in piling up a total of 292 and three touchdowns, plus a tipped interception.

The big plays came early and often. Running back Jaylen Warren took the first pass of the game for a 30-yard gain en route to piling up 176 yards from scrimmage.

Tight end Darnell Washington had a 47-yard catch. Receiver Roman Wilson added a 38-yard touchdown. Tight end Pat Freiermuth and receiver Ben Skowronek added receptions of at least 20 yards of their own.

It was a sharp contrast to what we've seen from McCarthy's offense since. Amid injuries to Wilson and fellow receiver Michael Pittman Jr., the playcalling has learned into the running game with Warren and a short-and-quick passing attack that's decent at moving the chains but not so great at piling up yardage in bunches.

It will therefore be interesting to see to what degree McCarthy tries to stick with what worked against the Bengals versus what's worked against the rest of the schedule so far.

The Steelers defense has smothered opposing running games. It's allowing an average of just 55 yards on the ground over the past four games.

The Bengals running back, however, has been kryptonite for the group over his past four outings against Pittsburgh.

He's averaged 6.25 yards per carry and totaled 338 yards over the span, which has forced the Steelers to respect the run while seeking principally to slow Burrow, Chase and Higgins.

Pittsburgh has benefitted from being able to make opposing offenses one dimensional, so keep an eye on the amount of balance Brown is able to give Cincinnati in this one.

Wisconsin's season-opening nine-game unbeaten streak – the best start for the men's hockey team in 45 years – ended Nov. 14 in a 2-1 loss to Ohio State at the Kohl Center.

Top-ranked Wisconsin (8-1-1, 4-1-1 Big Ten) also suffered a setback when goaltender Daniel Hauser ended up on the bottom of a pile during the first OSU goal late in the first period. Houser started to get up and then shook his head and stayed down for several moments before being helped off.

Alexis Couroyer, who has split time with Hauser, finished the game with 14 saves over 41-plus minutes after picking up the win a night earlier.

Ohio State (4-6-0, 2-2-0 Big Ten) got goals from Thomas Weis, a senior from Madison, in the first period and Felix Caron in the second. JJ Wiebusch scored the Badgers' lone goal 8 minutes into the third period in front of a season-high crowd of 12,193.

Buckeyes goaltender Jakub Milota, a freshman from the Czech Republic, made 27 saves after suffering a 5-2 defeat the previous night.

"You learn the most about your group when you've had some adversity, and we had some adversity tonight," coach Mike Hastings said. "So we'll continue to learn"

#2729. JJ Redick has lofty defensive identity for Lakers: ‘Physical as f–k’

We all know JJ Redick is a basketball sicko.

You know, the type of guy who rewatches games in a dark basement to pore over what he and the Lakers could've done better.

On Friday, we got a glimpse of what his staff is doing behind the scenes.

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick looks on during the first half of an NBA basketball game against the Milwaukee Bucks, Nov. 11, 2026, in Milwaukee. AP Photo/Aaron Gash

Redick said his analytics team used the three-day break between games to prepare a 21-page presentation on the Lakers, who have won seven games in a row and have the NBA's best record at 11-2.

The coaches reviewed it for 1 ½ hours on Friday and presented it to the players.

"Being first in the West, with the stuff that they showed us, you would think we were almost last, you know?" Ziaire Williams said, flashing a smile. "But gotta keep us honest."

"We know we want to be a top-10 defense," Redick said. "We know we are not going to be able to do that unless we become better than a bottom-10 transition team and better than a bottom-10 defensive rebounding team."

While the Lakers are leading the league in steals per game (11), are third in blocks per game (6.2) and are second in total deflections (257), they're greatly struggling in other areas defensively.

The Lakers are rated 18th defensively and 26th in rebounding (40.8).

Redick also identified a key area on transition defense he wants to tweak.

"Some of the transition stuff is live-ball turnovers," Redick said. "We're at a 10% live-ball turnover rate. So one out of every 10 possessions is a live-ball turnover that's going to create a transition possession."

Despite being the top-rated team in the league offensively, the Lakers have multiple areas in which they want to improve, including bolstering their third unit, which has notoriously squandered leads late in games.

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick and Luka Doncic converse with referee James Williams during a game against the Atlanta Hawks on Nov. 9, 2026. Getty Images

Redick pointed out that Cameron Carr and Adou Thiero are still playing catch-up after missing time due to various injuries.

Lakers assistant coach Scott Brooks is trying to get them up to speed.

"He took those guys for a classroom setting [Friday]," Redick said. "We just need to coach them more. Not going to put it all on them. They need to be able to run offense, though.

"I think that's the biggest thing. It's unacceptable to just consistently be calling offensive plays and then they come down and jack a 3 with 18 on the shot clock. We're trying to use time and be organized."

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick reacts on the sidelines during a game against the Atlanta Hawks in Atlanta on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Redick, whom the Lakers hired to take over the helm in June 2024 despite having no prior coaching experience, has shined in his role.

He led the Lakers to back-to-back 50-win seasons for the first time since Phil Jackson in 2007-2011.

He has a clear idea of what he wants the Lakers' identity to be on both sides of the court.

"Organized, unselfish and advantage-based," he said.

"Organized, physical as f–k and relentless," he added.

#2725. LIVE! Harrison Vs. Nunes Full Fight Results, Streaming Updates

The greatest Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) women's fight of all-time (not my words) has finally arrived …

Bantamweight legends Kayla Harrison vs. Amanda Nunes are finally set to collide tonight (Sat., Nov. 14, 2026) inside Madison Square Garden in New York, N.Y., at UFC 334.

Harrison talked the talk while running the PFL table (aside from that "best-ever loss" to Larissa Pacheco). And since crossing into the Octagon, she's walked the walk. Oddly, Harrison has only competed twice as a UFC fighter coming into tonight (here's why); however, she has finished two former champions and captured gold in the process.

That was seemingly enough to lure "Lioness" out of self-imposed retirement.

Nunes dominated UFC's 135-pound division for most of a decade, walking away on top just a couple of years ago. If anyone can return from retirement and immediately reclaim the throne, it is Nunes (and Georges St-Pierre, of course!). Harrison, however, represents a super tough task at any point in Nunes' career … and there are plenty of questions heading into this showdown about how Harrison will perform following neck surgery.

We are about to get some awesome answers.

Checkout how the highly-anticipated championship clash between two generations of women's Bantamweight greatness unfolds below:

Nunes, the challenger, made the walk to the Octagon first, looking to be in great physical shape after such a long layoff. Harrison, the champion, came out to Rocky-themed "Eye of the Tiger," which hopefully woke up the poor "Big Apple" crowd after a lackluster main card. Both badasses touched gloves as a mutual sign of respect and we were off and punching … Nunes threw the first strike, a left jab, but caught nothing but air. She tried to follow up with a looping right hand, but pulled it back as Harrison circled away from danger. Nunes continued to hold her ground, scoring with a nice shovel uppercut, then a kick to the body as Harrison looked to close the distance. Harrison tried to grab a hold of Nunes, but ate a big shot on the way in. Harrison tried again, was in on a single-leg, but Nunes made her pay once again. The pair returned to their feet and Harrison was able to mush her against the cage, finally, but Nunes squirmed out. Harrison landed a nice left hand, and moments later, hip-tossed Nunes and had her trapped in a crucifix position, dropping short hammer fists across her face. There wasn't much on them, but Nunes was trapped bad and the referee was locked in to make sure it didn't get too bad for the Brazilian. Harrison trapped Nunes' arm — full crucifix down the stretch — to probably take the round late after a rocky start (pun intended).

Nunes was all smiles coming out for the second stanza despite the awful position she found herself late in the opening frame. She pressured Harrison on the feet, then tried to take her down, before pressing her against the fence. Nunes attempted another takedown along the cage, for some unknown reason, giving Harrison exactly what she wanted. Nunes landed some knees in the clinch, but it seemed like Harrison was just looking for the right angle to send her for another ride. But, it didn't come; instead, Nunes chopped Harrison down to a knee, then got behind her, only for Harrison to uncork a tricky trip that landed her on top of Nunes with two minutes on the clock. Harrison had Nunes in a front head lock, in side control, and began to rain down short shots. Nunes tried to buck out, while Harrison landed some nice ground-and-pound from the crucifix position once again. She attempted a kimura, but Nunes was able to defend, only to eat more short shots to the face. It was another good start for Nunes, and another great finish for Harrison — 2-0 champ heading into the third.

Nunes needed to do something different here to turn the tide. She pumped a left jab early, then a straight right hand to the body as Harrison countered with a weak left hook. Nunes, once again, was the aggressor on another takedown, but this time she gave up rather than pursuing it when it wasn't going her way. Nunes, in a scramble, was able to toss Harrison to the canvas moments later, then in the scramble, was able to land in full mount with Harrison in a seated position. Harrison was able to get to her knees after threatening with a choke, which she used to get back to her feet, drilling her with knees to the body on the way up. Nunes continued to grapple, taking Harrison's back and getting her hooks in as Harrison turned into Nunes and out of danger. Harrison ended up in full guard, dropping a hard elbow on Nunes' jaw once she was able to get her bearings. Another big elbow cut Nunes over the eyebrow. Harrison continued with the ground-and-pound, landing a huge shot down the stretch that may or may not have stolen her the round — 2-1 Harrison, possibly 3-0.

Harrison's corner implored her to win round four, perhaps realizing the third frame was close and she was getting fatigued. Both ladies looked a little slower 15 minutes in, with nothing really happening in the first 60 seconds. Nice right hand from Nunes, but Harrison was quick to tie her up. Nunes went for a kick, Harrison caught it, and as Nunes tried to free her limb, Harrison landed on her back. And literally seconds later, she sunk in a rear-naked choke with Nuens on her knees and "Lioness" was tapping before her belly even touched the canvas.

#2724. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2720. Juice your growth and save on taxes in this workplace investment account

Workers are in the heart of open enrollment season for next year's benefits, and rising healthcare costs are shining a spotlight on an offering that includes a tax-advantaged investment account.

Healthcare expenses are climbing for workers and employers alike, with average total family premiums, including the employer's share, averaging $28,303, up 5% from a year ago, according to data from health policy organization KFF, formerly the Kaiser Family Foundation.

To manage the costs, a growing number of employers are moving to high-deductible health plans, which work alongside health savings accounts or HSAs. Almost 40% of companies with at least 10 employees that offer health benefits also have an HSA-qualified plan, KFF found.

Health savings accounts have three major tax advantages. First, contributions that your employer automatically deducts from your pay aren't taxed. Second, money stashed into the HSA grows free of taxes. Finally, you can make tax-free withdrawals for qualified health expenses – just be sure to save your receipts.

"I love HSAs because of their triple-tax advantage," said Eileen Olson, CFP and founder of Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, near Savannah, Georgia. "For people who can afford to leave it alone, it can be one of the best retirement accounts they're going to have."

In 2027, those with individual healthcare coverage through a high-deductible plan can stash up to $4,500 in an HSA, including any contributions from employers. That number goes up to $9,000 for family plans. Individuals can kick in a catch-up contribution of $1,000 if they're aged 55 and older and not enrolled in Medicare.

The HSA differs from the healthcare flexible spending account, known as the FSA.

FSA funds must be used by the end of the plan year unless your employer allows a carryover of up to $700 or an additional 2.5 months to use the money. HSAs, however, have no expiration date on their funds – and that's what makes them such a powerful tool for long-term planning. You can also take the HSA with you if you change employers.

"Get the money deployed, take advantage of the pretax contribution, and allocate the money into a growth portfolio," said Mark Stancato, certified financial planner at VIP Wealth Advisors in Decatur, Georgia. "With the HSA, you can keep compounding year over year."

The structure of an HSA and the available investment menu will vary from one plan to the next, and some will require that employees keep some of their holdings in cash.

Preset HSA fund menus tend to have 15 to 25 funds to choose from, and providers say that accountholders who invest tend to use two to four funds, according to Greg Carlson, senior research analyst for equity strategies at Morningstar.

How you allocate your HSA will depend on several factors, including your family's health prospects in the next year, your cash flow needs – how much you can comfortably sock into the HSA – and your risk tolerance, said André Small, CFP and founder of A Small Investment in Houston.

Small's standard is to keep an amount equal to 120% of the plan's out-of-pocket maximum held in cash in the HSA.

"That covers a bad year without forcing a sale at the wrong time," he said. "Above that amount? I typically advise investing the amount the client is comfortable investing, allocated to their risk tolerance, their time horizon and the goal of spending these dollars on care later."

For 2027, the IRS defines a high-deductible plan as one with an annual deductible no less than $1,750 for self-only coverage ($3,500 for family plans) and with an out-of-pocket expense limit that doesn't exceed $8,700 for self-only (or $17,400 for family coverage). Out-of-pocket expenses include deductibles, copays and other costs – but not premiums.

Other advisors suggest having up to the deductible in cash, though some HSA plan providers require a stated minimum amount in cash.

Beyond this cash reserve, financial advisors recommend allocating into stocks.

Patrick Swift, CFP and president of Amplius Wealth Advisors in Blue Bell, Pennsylvania, aims for an allocation of up to 60% in U.S. large cap stocks, 20% in small and mid-cap stocks and 20% in international stocks.

"We believe the equity portfolio should be well diversified," he said. "If the [HSA] balance is 2% to 10% of your net worth, why not be aggressive? That can change based on the situation, but if you are comfortable with the philosophical aspect, why not be growth oriented?"

Similarly, Stancato likes to go heavy on equity exposure in HSA accounts. "I allocate more dollars into small caps and emerging markets – those asset classes with more volatility but also more opportunity for growth," the advisor said. He also adds some large-cap domestic exposure.

For the adventurous, select HSA providers are offering brokerage window access, meaning investors can pick from a broader array of investments, including individual stocks.

This year, seven providers surveyed by Morningstar offer access to brokerage windows – up from four in 2023 – including HealthEquity, Fidelity and Lively. Be aware that there may be annual fees attached, either a flat dollar amount or a percentage of assets.

Rachel Elson, a CFP and wealth advisor at Perigon Wealth Management in San Francisco, recommends keeping things simple. "You can do a three-ETF model, covering some allocation that includes the U.S. market, and two ETFs for developed and emerging markets."

"You don't need to get super complicated here," she added.

#2719. ESPN announces decision on Rex Ryan after arrest

Former NFL head coach and current ESPN analyst Rex Ryan is facing six charges in connection with an alleged hit-and-run in Nashville. But it doesn't sound like he will be missing any time on ESPN.

The network says the former New York Jets head coach is still set to appear as scheduled this weekend, including on Sunday NFL Countdown, despite his arrest and the pending charges.

Police say Ryan struck two pedestrians with his pickup truck in a crosswalk on Broadway in downtown Nashville just before midnight on Nov. 5. After reviewing surveillance footage, police filed six warrants against him.

The charges include leaving the scene of an accident, failure to give information or render aid, and failure to obey a traffic control signal. Ryan turned himself in on Wednesday, was released on a $6,000 bond, and is due in court on Dec. 18.

One of the alleged victims, attorney Michael Holland, said Ryan "almost killed" him and his wife. He claimed Ryan ran over both of their feet, confronted them when they caught up to him in traffic, and then drove off.

"He was told in no uncertain terms what he had done, and instead of staying at the scene or even saying, 'Sorry,' he just got back in his vehicle and took off," Holland said, via the New York Post.

Ryan's attorney declined to comment on the allegations.

Despite the charges, ESPN doesn't appear to be making any changes. A network spokesperson told Richard Deitsch that Ryan will make his appearance as planned on Sunday morning.

"As of now, Rex will appear as scheduled, including on Sunday NFL Countdown," the spokesperson said, via Deitsch.

Deitsch added that he "would not expect Ryan to address the matter on air."

Ryan has been an analyst at ESPN since 2017, appearing regularly on Sunday NFL Countdown and Get Up. The words "as of now" obviously leave room for things to change. But for this Sunday, at least, it sounds like Ryan will remain on the air for the network despite the incident.

#2716. The Suns are getting crushed in one critical area of the game

When you look at the Phoenix Suns and see a 5-6 record staring back at you, there are plenty of explanations for why they've stumbled out of the gate. One of the most obvious is the schedule. According to ESPN's strength-of-schedule metrics, Phoenix has faced the third-toughest slate in the NBA through the first 11 games of the season. We can also point to the ongoing challenges surrounding Jalen Green and his inability to consistently find his place on this roster. We can discuss how Miles Bridges has yet to hit his stride as he continues adjusting to a new team, a new system, and new responsibilities.

But there's one glaring deficiency that threatens to haunt the Suns throughout the entire season unless they fundamentally change their approach or somehow miraculously become a larger basketball team overnight. Their inability to impact the game at the rim. And the numbers are downright horrific.

Last season, Phoenix finished 29th in the NBA in field goal attempts within five feet of the basket, averaging 23.7 per game. This season? They're averaging 23.5, the fifth fewest in the league. Think about that for a moment. The Suns have a healthy Jalen Green, a player whose athleticism and explosiveness theoretically provide the ability to get downhill and attack the basket. They also brought in Miles Bridges, another player expected to provide a more physical presence and generate opportunities around the rim. And through 11 games, neither addition has meaningfully moved the needle. Phoenix is attacking the basket at essentially the same rate as last season, despite investing significant resources in players who were supposed to address that very deficiency.

But the offensive struggles around the cylinder are only half the problem. The other half? Rebounding. And somehow, the numbers are even uglier.

The Suns rank dead last in the NBA in rebounds per game, averaging a miserable 38.9. That's a full 10 rebounds fewer than the Minnesota Timberwolves, who lead the league at 48.9 per game. Phoenix also ranks 30th in rebounding percentage at 45.2%, meaning opponents are consistently winning the battle for available rebounds.

When you begin examining how that translates into actual points, the situation becomes even more alarming. The Suns surrender 18.1 second-chance points per game, the second most in the league. Meanwhile, they're generating only 12.8 second-chance points themselves, the second fewest. So not only are opponents getting additional opportunities to score, but Phoenix is failing to create those same opportunities on the other end. That's a pretty brutal combination.

If you need a recent example of how dire the situation has become, look no further than Thursday night's victory over Charlotte. Oso Ighodaro and Khaman Maluach, two of the players Phoenix relies upon to provide some semblance of interior presence, combined for five rebounds. In a game where the Suns were outrebounded by 21.

No matter how you slice it, this is a five-alarm fire for a team attempting to establish itself as a legitimate competitor in the Western Conference. Much like speed, size can't be taught. You can preach positioning, emphasize boxing out, and demand greater effort on the glass, but there's only so much coaching can accomplish when your roster consistently finds itself at a physical disadvantage.

The most deflating aspect of this deficiency is how it impacts both ends of the floor. Defensively, the Suns can execute an entire possession correctly, rotate effectively, contest shots, and force opponents into difficult attempts. But if they can't secure the rebound, all that work becomes meaningless. The possession continues, the defense has to scramble again, and another opportunity is handed to the opposition. You cannot consistently give NBA teams extra possessions and expect to win basketball games. It places an enormous burden on your defense, especially when you're already asking players to compensate for a lack of size and interior physicality.

And offensively, the inability to consistently attack and finish around the basket creates an entirely different set of problems. When opposing defenses don't have to respect your ability to penetrate and score at the rim, they can become more aggressive on the perimeter. They can close out harder, pressure ball handlers, and force you into difficult jump shots because they aren't particularly concerned about what happens if you get past the initial defender. Perhaps that also helps explain why Phoenix is averaging the second-fewest free throw attempts per game in the NBA. They're not getting to the rack.

It's an unsustainable combination of deficiencies, particularly for a team that doesn't possess the overwhelming offensive firepower to compensate for them. The Suns can survive a difficult schedule. They can work through the growing pains associated with integrating new players. They can experiment with rotations, redefine responsibilities, and hope that chemistry improves as the season progresses. But how exactly do you overcome being one of the worst teams in basketball at attacking the rim, rebounding the basketball, and preventing opponents from generating second-chance opportunities?

That's a much more difficult question to answer. And right now, I'm not sure the Phoenix Suns have one.

I'm trying to find a little optimism in all of this. The Suns are 5-6, they've played one of the toughest schedules in the league, and they have plenty of areas that need improvement. But we're still early enough in the season for adjustments to matter. Jalen Green can find his footing. Miles Bridges can become more comfortable in his role. The coaching staff can experiment with lineups and find better ways to generate opportunities around the basket.

None of that is guaranteed to solve the rebounding problem, and the lack of size remains a legitimate concern. But this team doesn't need to become a dominant interior force overnight. It needs to become more competitive in the areas that are currently costing it possessions and points. If Phoenix can make even modest progress there, there's still plenty of season left to build something worthwhile. The problems are real, but so is the opportunity to get better.

#2710. Blue Jay volleyball makes history, stuns Bismarck Century

Nov. 14—JAMESTOWN — Members of the 2026 Jamestown High School volleyball team wanted to accomplish two things this season.

"WDA championship and State championship, that's what our goal has been all year," said JHS senior libero Adisyn Yunck in a previous interview on Oct. 20. "(Head coach) Sara (Hegerle) said first practice of the season, 'what is our goal as a team?' Immediately we said, 'both championships — we are getting those.'"

The WDA championship has since been secured.

Yunck and company earned Jamestown's first-ever West Region volleyball tournament championship on Saturday. The Blue Jays topped 12-time defending region champion Bismarck Century 3-2. It was the first time Jamestown had beaten Century this season.

"We've played well before and it hasn't ended up like this for us," Hegerle said. "It's like, am I dreaming right now? But I am not. It's real and it's good. It's the first time in the history of Blue Jay volleyball. I am glad to be a part of it. I am glad I didn't get in the way and I am so glad this team gets to experience what hard work looks like if you keep with it. It's paying off right now."

After the Blue Jays dropped the first set 25-10 and finished the set with only five kills, the Jays totally flipped the script, and surged out to a 17-6 lead over the Patriots.

"That first set, we just needed to get all of the jitters out," JHS senior outside hitter Lucy Falk said. "I had to get into the groove kind of and get in the mind-set for the game. We knew going into the rest of the game that we had to control our side of the net and have that push (Century) and have Century react to us. We just kept trying to control our side to push them."

Stellar plays from Hannah Attleson helped the Jays get three points away from the win in the second set. The senior setter saved three balls then delivered the kill shot to make it 22-12. A discombobulated Century offense had an attack error on the next point to make it 23-12. Century saved two match points but it was too little too late. Amelia Newman secured the second set win with an attack that skidded off the block and landed in.

The Jays started the third strong with a 4-0 advantage but the Patriots came back, putting together a 5-1 run to tie the game at 5-5.

Falk gave Jamestown a 18-17 lead, with a smart attack against the outside blockers. Jamestown kept swinging and scoring which led to a 22-19 advantage and a timeout from Century head coach Jamie Zastoupil.

Century scored three unanswered to tie it and on a Jamestown attack error the Patriots took a 23-22 lead. Century ended the third with a 2-1 run.

"After the third set, we just said, this is the moment we've been waiting for so we just need to push the next two sets," Falk said. "We had nothing to lose."

Jamestown topped Century 25-17 in the fourth then came out swinging and secured the first two points of the final set.

Century got on the board by way of an attack but Falk made it 3-1 with a smash on the outside. Century point No. 2 on a Jamestown service error but then allowed a 3-0 run by the Jays to make it 6-2.

The Patriot's 6-foot-5 freshman, Lily Edinger, got her team a side out out of a timeout but Falk went right back to work, securing another kill and point for Jamestown. Century gave Jamestown another point by way of an attack error to make it 8-3.

Century notched back-to-back attacks to make it 8-5 and was close to making it 8-6 before Claire Iverson blocked Edinger and made it 9-5 Blue Jays. On the next play, Claire Marker zipped one down the middle and Century called another timeout.

A service error on Jamestown made it 10-6 but the Jays remained calm and steady down the stretch Newman secured the next point by way of a kill. The Jays then took advantage of back-to-back errors by Century.

"They were determined that, (losing to Century) wasn't going to happen again," Hegerle said. "Century is a good team. Legacy is a good team and we have proven we are a good team. I am so proud of how they fought through hard things and came out on top."

Up 13-6, Jamestown missed a serve which was followed by another attack by the Patriots. Claire Marker made it 14-8 with another blazer down the middle and while the Patriots saved that particular match point, they couldn't mount a comeback.

On the final point of the match, Attleson set up Falk and the senior scored.

"I wasn't feeling confident until close to the end of the fifth set," Falk said. "There's been times when we've let up at the end of a set when we've been up so I knew we had to stay focused until the very last point. ... (When the ball came to me) I knew I just had to be aggressive and swing as hard as I could. I couldn't believe it when it hit the floor. We've been waiting for this moment so for it to be actually happening is just so surreal."

The senior along with Attleson, Newman and Marker were named to the All-WDA team at the conclusion of the tournament. Falk led the Jays in offensive efforts against the Patriots with 23 kills. The senior finished the WDA tournament with 70 kills, Marker posted 16 kills. Newman ended the WDA championship match with nine kills, one assist, 26 digs and three aces. Attleson dished out 49 assists had four kills, nine digs and an ace.

"All of them are well-deserving," Hegerle said of her four All-Region players. "We could have probably had one or two more. Marker only played half of a year. That just goes to show her impact. Her impact on the bench is almost as important as what she does on the court. I am really happy for her."

Falk was named the West Region Senior Athlete of the Year while Hegerle picked up WDA Coach of the Year honors.

"That seems like a no-brainer, but there are so many good players in the West," Hegerle said. "That wasn't an automatic but it was unanimous."

At the 2026 NDHSAA Division AA Volleyball State Tournament the Blue Jays are set to face fourth-seeded Fargo Shanley at 3 p.m. on Thursday, Nov. 19 at the Bismarck Events Center.

"I am really excited, knowing that we have set ourselves up for success," Falk said. "Now we just have to work hard when we get there."

Sunday’s game in Germany will be the first one against the Patriots with a coach other than Bill Belichick. Goff has never faced current Patriots coach Mike Vrabel; during Goff’s time as a starter with the Rams and Lions and Vrabel’s tenure with the Titans, their two teams never crossed paths.

Goff’s first loss to New England came in 2016, in his third career start. The Patriots won, 26-10. Two years later, New England beat Goff and the Rams in the Super Bowl, 13-3.

In 2020, Goff and the Rams beat the Patriots, 24-3. In 2022, the Patriots beat Goff and the Lions, 29-0.

Sunday’s game is consequential for both teams. The 6-2 Lions are caught in a cluster of four NFC North teams that all have six or more wins. The Patriots, at 5-4, are fading in the AFC East race and could be scrambling to secure a wild-card spot.

#2696. An Eagles rookie progress report at the midway point of 2026 season

An Eagles rookie progress report at the midway point of 2026 season originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Eagles had high expectations entering this season but are sitting at 2-7 at the bye week.

Now it's time to see what the young players can do.

The Eagles drafted eight players in April and seven of them have seen game action over the first half of the season, but to varying degrees.

With the Eagles on their Week 10 bye week, let's recap the first half of the season for all eight of their draft picks:

After some disappointing moments early in his rookie season, we have seen a ton of growth from Makai Lemon recently. Without DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks for three weeks, Lemon has had the three best games of his rookie season against the Cowboys (7 catches for 67 yards, 1 TD), Commanders (6 catches for 57 yards) and Giants (6 catches for 61 yards). While Lemon was tough on himself for a couple drops in Week 9, he has been one of the few bright spots recently.

Through nine games, Lemon has been targeted 54 times and has 37 catches for 312 yards and a touchdown. He's on pace for 102 targets, 70 catches, 589 yards and 2 touchdowns. But it's also worth noting that his numbers have been improving as the season goes on.

Here's a look at the Eagles' rookie records for receptions and receiving yards. Lemon is on pace to finish his season second on the receptions list and ninth in receiving yards. But hopefully the Eagles have scrapped all those behind-the-line passes to him.

Through nine weeks, Lemon is tied with KC Conception for the lead among rookies in receptions and is fourth in receiving yards among rookies behind Denzel Boston (507), Concepcion (437) and Carnell Tate (413).

After a rough training camp, Eli Stowers dealt with a quad injury that kept him on IR for the first six weeks of the season. He made his NFL debut a few weeks ago against the Cowboys, but hasn't played a ton on offense yet. Here's a look at his offensive snap counts for these last three weeks.

Week 7 vs. DAL: 12 snapsWeek 8 at WAS: 13 snapsWeek 9 vs. NYG: 7 snaps

Overall, Stowers has been targeted 5 times and has 3 catches for 53 yards. All three of those catches came in the loss to Washington and two of them came very late in the fourth quarter. His long of 34 yards came at the very end of the game.

But Stowers hasn't looked out of place in limited action. He has been doing some good things away from the football and has shown a real willingness to do some dirty work and block. While blocking is probably never going to be his strength, he needed to improve in that area and is clearly working on it. But in this lost season, it would make sense to see more of Stowers in the second half.

In addition to his work on offense, Stowers has also played 27 special teams snaps. That's something new for him because he began his college career as a quarterback and then became a star tight end. But he's working hard at that too.

The plan was for Markel Bell to sit all season and learn behind Jordan Mailata and Lane Johnson. But that plan got tossed in the garbage can early this season when Johnson abruptly retired. Bell was thrust into the starting lineup in Week 4 against the Rams and has started the last six games with plenty of ups and downs.

Early in his time as a starter, Bell looked really promising and looked to be settling into that role. But the last couple of games have been much rougher for the 6-foot-9 rookie. In six starts this season, according to ProFootballFocus, Bell has given up 5 sacks and 19 pressures, but 3 of those sacks came in his late-notice start against the Rams in Week 4.

There's a really good chance that veteran Fred Johnson would be a better option right now, but the Eagles should ride this out with Bell to figure out if he really has the potential to be a long-term replacement for Johnson. We'll probably learn a lot about him over the second half of this season.

Round 5-178: Cole Payton, QB, North Dakota State

The Eagles made sure to give Cole Payton plenty of reps in training camp despite having three quarterbacks on the depth chart ahead of him. But Payton has been inactive five times this season and has been active but hasn't played three times. Back in Week 5 against the Jaguars, Payton played 10 snaps on special teams and that's the only time he has seen the field.

The idea of Payton on special teams is fun, especially in a lost season like this. Maybe the Eagles will get him some more reps in that role or perhaps find a way to get him on the field on offense. Joe Milton and Tanner McKee are both still ahead of Payton on the depth chart but the way this season is going, would you be surprised to see Payton eventually get on the field as a starter?

When the Eagles drafted Micah Morris in the sixth round, he was expected to be a developmental pick and that has held true. Through 9 games, Morris has played one snap on offense and 19 on special teams. Morris has been active the last seven weeks but hasn't needed to play. If this season continues to spiral, maybe we'll get to see what Morris can do.

Because Cole Wisniewski missed most of training camp with injuries (hamstring and concussion), he never really had much of a shot to make the Eagles' 53-man roster. Through nine games, Wisniewski has been elevated twice and has played 36 snaps on special teams. He has one elevation remaining.
