#2637. ‘I believe in myself’: Lincoln Riley defends himself despite another disappointing season

Lincoln Riley's fifth season at USC was supposed to be the year the Trojans finally broke through. Instead, USC is once again on the outside looking in when it comes to the College Football Playoff. Despite the loss, Riley made it clear that he still believes in himself.

After Saturday's loss to Indiana knocked USC out of the playoff race, the embattled head coach made it clear that he still believes in himself and the direction of the program.

USC fell 27-13 to No. 9 Indiana in Bloomington, dropping to 7-3 on the season and 4-3 in Big Ten play. That officially ended the Trojans' playoff hopes, meaning Riley will go five straight seasons at USC without a playoff berth.

That's a far cry from Riley's time at Oklahoma, where he led the Sooners to the playoff in 2017, 2018, and 2019. And the pressure has been building all season.

Paul Finebaum called for USC to fire Riley in September, saying "everybody knows who the fraud is." Kalshi's market on Riley's future also gave him better-than-even odds of being fired, with about a 67% chance at one point that he would be out by Feb. 1, 2027.

To make matters worse, crosstown rival UCLA entered the weekend undefeated at 10-0 in Bob Chesney's first season, putting the Bruins on track for a playoff berth in his first season with the team.

After the game, Riley reaffirmed his belief in himself and the program. He didn't sound like a coach worried about his job.

"I believe in what we're doing. I believe in myself," Riley said, via On3. "I believe in our leadership. I believe in our administration. I believe in everything that's happening here. Trust me, there's nobody that wants it as bad as all of us involved."

Riley also insisted that USC isn't far from where it wants to be.

"We know how close we are as a group, and we know how close we are as a team. We got a good view of that tonight. We will keep battling. We will get there and all this will continue to make it more sweet when that time does happen," Riley continued.

USC fans have been hearing that for five years now. And with UCLA rising across town, Riley may be running out of time to prove it.

#2636. While tied for NBA's best record, Lakers believe they can be better

While rocketing toward the top of the league, the Lakers have been far from perfect. That's good news to them.

"A big thing that we talk with our players about a lot is being able to learn and get better and try to correct things even when you are winning," coach JJ Redick said.

The Lakers (11-2) have won seven consecutive games entering Sunday's 1 p.m. PST matinee against the Suns (5-6) in Phoenix.

Using a rare multiple-day break between games to audit their performances, coaches and analytics staffers showed slide presentations to players about both offensive and defensive flaws this week. The lectures left the team with one of the best records in the league feeling as if it was one of the worst, forward Ziaire Williams joked.

Already the top-ranked offense in the league, the Lakers should strive to match that by becoming a top-10 defense, Redick implored his team. Williams is not stopping there.

"Top 10 should be at least like our standard, if not better," the forward said. "Our half-court defense has been great. Obviously, rebounding has been one of the biggest things for us, cleaning up transition as well. But the potential's there. We have the size, the length, the athleticism. It's just about going out there and executing."

Read more: Lakers' Austin Reaves considered day-to-day with heel injury

The Lakers, ranked 18th in defensive efficiency, thrive on forcing turnovers and protecting the rim. Their 18.5 turnovers forced per game rank third in the league, and they average an NBA-best 11 steals per game. Center Walker Kessler's 2.2 blocks per game rank third.

But they can't finish the strong half-court possessions. The Lakers are ranked 28th in defensive rebounding and 25th in second-chance points given up.

The Lakers staff rewatched every offensive rebound given up this season. Lack of boxing out was the biggest fault. Then there were instances when players stood and watched.

"If I stand and watch and try and outjump someone else, I'm probably not going to get the rebound," said forward Jake LaRavia, who has been an offensive rebounding revelation since entering the starting lineup, averaging 2.8 offensive rebounds in the last nine games. "So you have to go and be physical and hit bodies, and then just be able to dive on loose balls, finish possessions, it's really just who's going to work harder."

Kessler is averaging 8.1 defensive rebounds during the Lakers' seven-game winning streak — which is the second-longest in Redick's coaching tenure — compared to 6.3 during the first six games.

Forward Jarred Vanderbilt, who did not play in the first four games, has made the most of his limited minutes off the bench, grabbing 7.9 defensive rebounds per 36 minutes, the second-best rate on the team among players who have played more than three minutes. Vanderbilt, averaging 3.8 rebounds per game in 11.9 minutes, had 10 rebounds in less than 14 minutes against the Detroit Pistons on Nov. 8.

Transition defense also is sinking the Lakers' defensive efforts. Opponents are scoring 20.2 points off turnovers per game, which put the Lakers 24th out of 30 teams. Redick blames some of that on the Lakers' offensive flaws. Although they are the league's most efficient offense, the Lakers turn the ball over 16.9 times per game, the fifth-most in the NBA.

Lakers guard Luka Doncic shoots over two Bucks during a win Wednesday in Milwaukee. (Aaron Gash / Associated Press)

Luka Doncic, the league's leading scorer at 38.6 points per game, also averages an NBA-worst five turnovers. Austin Reaves, who is day-to-day because of a left heel bruise suffered Wednesday against Milwaukee, averages 24.7 points and 3.4 turnovers.

Doncic is expected to play Sunday despite tweaking his right ankle late in Wednesday's win. Reaves didn't participate in practice Saturday but Collin Sexton was a full participant. The guard wore a thick Band-Aid over his right eyebrow and had bruising around his right eye after bumping heads with Milwaukee's Ryan Rollins but said he doesn't expect to wear a mask. He needs only to keep the cut covered to ensure it doesn't open up again. The rugged guard is familiar with the protocols; Sexton said this was the 11th time in his career that he's received stitches in his face.

The short break offered an important opportunity for players to rest after a grueling three-game Eastern Conference trip. They now enter a softer stretch in the schedule. After Sunday's game in Phoenix, the Lakers play their next four at home against three teams — Charlotte, Sacramento and Utah, twice — that have a combined six wins.

Their next game against a team with a winning record isn't until Nov. 27 at San Antonio. The 11-2 Spurs, who have won 11 consecutive games, are the only team with an active winning streak longer than the Lakers'.

#2633. Independent experts to review handling of Jalen Hurts’ blood clot situation as NFL gives insight into process

How the investigation into the circumstances around Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts' blood clots will proceed is coming into focus.

Independent experts will look at the matter and share their findings with the NFL and NFLPA. The Eagles' Super Bowl MVP quarterback is expected to sit out the remainder of the 2026 season after doctors discovered multiple blood clots in his lungs.

In response to an October letter from Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, the NFL provided additional information to her office about the review, which has not officially begun.

"As outlined by the league and NFLPA's Collective Bargaining Agreement, mutually agreed-upon independent medical experts will review the matter and share their conclusions and recommendations with both parties," Jeff Miller, NFL executive vice president of communications, public affairs and policy, said in a statement released by Blunt Rochester's office Friday.

Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts (1) takes the snap against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Hurts was first said to have a superficial blood clot before the Eagles faced the Jaguars in London in Week 5, but still played in the game. He flew home with the team and practiced fully the following Wednesday.

A follow-up test showed the clot had moved, leading to the 28-year-old being placed on injured reserve on Oct. 17 with a diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary emboli.

Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts (1) takes the snap from center Jake Majors (75) against the Jacksonville Jaguars, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026, in Tottenham. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The union called for a full investigation into the matter on Oct. 20, but it has not asked for a formal investigation into the health, safety or medical care provided by club-affiliated personnel, which it can under the CBA.

"The NFLPA is not aware of any NFL investigation into the medical care provided to Jalen Hurts," the NFLPA said in the statement last month. "In fact, the league previously informed the union that it did not plan to review the care he received. Before conclusions are drawn about how this situation was handled, there must be a full investigation into what occurred. Determining the facts is essential to ensuring players receive the highest level of care and protection going forward."

The neutral physicians selected must issue a written report within 60 days of being appointed. Both parties must act on those recommendations to address and correct any issues.

#2630. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2629. 3 Eagles tidbits coming out of the NFL trade deadline

NFL insiders Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport shared an NFL trade deadline notebook on ESPN that featured several mentions of the Philadelphia Eagles. Let's take a look at those here.

While the Eagles traded stars in Davis and center Cam Jurgens in the flurry leading up to the deadline, they held off trading another player who was wanted — Dallas Goedert. Sources said several teams inquired about the pass-catching tight end, including the 49ers. But Goedert, 31, never got close to being traded. He remains in Philadelphia and could even re-sign with the Eagles for 2027.

Not exactly shocking to see that teams had interest in acquiring him. Goedert is a solid tight end who could make nice contributions to a contending team.

At the same time, the Eagles didn't need to give him away for meager compensation. Especially when accounting for his salary cap ramifications.

It's interesting to see mention of the Eagles potentially keeping Goedert beyond 2026. It felt like the Eagles were close to moving on from him after each of the past two seasons. And he turns 32 in January. Are the two sides really going to do another one-year bandaid contract?

Maybe. The only Eagles tight end currently under contract beyond this season is … Eli Stowers. It wouldn't be very wise for the team to put all of their eggs in the basket of him panning out since the 2026 second-round pick has yet to show promise thus far.

The two teams that were most aggressive in trading for Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis were the Bills and Jaguars, who wound up trading a first- and second-round pick to the Eagles.

Interested to know exactly what the Bills were offering for Davis.

Nevertheless, seems like there was a bidding war for the Eagles' interior defender, which helps to explain why Howie Roseman was able to get such a big return from the jags.

The Eagles were not pleased that the Bengals reneged on their deal for Ebiketie after learning they would lose a third-round compensatory pick […]

Understandably so. The Eagles thought they had a done deal with the Bengals to ship out Ebiketie for a 2027 sixth-round pick.

Before it became official, however, Cincy realized (thanks to compensatory picks expert Nick Korte) that acquiring Ebiketie would cause him to forfeit the 2027 third-round pick comp pick they were set to earn for losing Trey Hendrickson.

While one can understand why the Bengals wanted to back out after realizing their mistake, this failed trade is a pretty bad look for them.

I feel like the Bengals owe the Eagles one. Not exactly sure what that looks like but it's in Cincy's own interests to maintain healthy working relationships with other NFL general managers.
